#473. France Riots Put Hollywood Shoots on Alert as Curfews Disrupt Movie Theaters: It ‘Has Now Been Flagged as a Problem Area’

In the same year that France has hosted two of television’s most glamorous and escapist international hits — the final season of Netflix’s “Emily in Paris” and Season 4 of HBO’s “The White Lotus” — the country has been shaken by one of its most violent waves of rioting in decades.

What began as nationwide demonstrations on Oct. 17 over the rising cost of living and deteriorating conditions in public schools descended into scenes of urban chaos. Some 550,000 people took to the streets and the protests turned into widespread looting, arson and clashes with police. Three days later, authorities had recorded 2,397 arrests, and at least 3,000 businesses have been damaged alongside landmarks. Related Stories Emmys Move to Prime Video in Six-Year, Global Deal Worth Around $15 Million a Year

In Lyon, rioters set fire to the historic tourist office on Place Bellecour. In Marseille, masked protesters stormed City Hall and toppled a bust of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic. In Paris, luxury boutiques were ransacked and storefronts smashed. Popular on Variety

Amid the post-apocalyptic spectacle, France has continued to serve as a playground for some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, notably in the French Riviera region, which is hosting the final stretch of filming on the fourth season of Mike White’s “The White Lotus.” Warner Bros.’ “Ocean” prequel, which Bradley Cooper is directing and starring in opposite Margot Robbie, George MacKay and Monica Barbaro, is wrapping its French shoot in Monaco; and Mimi Cave’s psychological thriller “Pumping Black,” starring Natalie Portman, Jonathan Bailey and Lukas Gage, is filming in Nice.

So far, these productions have largely escaped disruption, but the riots have rattled film crews and prompted warnings from Hollywood studios’ security departments.

Veteran French executive producer Raphaël Benoliel, who is currently working on “Pumping Black” in Nice, says the American team was concerned about violence even though the shoot hasn’t been disrupted so far.

“The Americans did ask, ‘Do you think it’s dangerous?’ We told them, ‘From where we are, we think it’s fine.’ And everything has been going smoothly,” Benoliel says.

But when it comes to upcoming shoots, the unrest might impact future decisions over destinations. “The studios’ internal security departments have clearly said, ‘Be careful. Avoid Paris. Avoid Marseille,’” Benoliel says. “That has been explicitly communicated. If you wanted to organize a location scout in Paris today or tomorrow, it’s entirely possible that a studio would say, ‘No, postpone it. Wait.’”

He continues, “Because of what happened, France has now been flagged as a problem area. You know how people say, ‘Don’t go filming in Ukraine right now,’ or in certain parts of the Middle East? Well, now France has been put on that list.”

Still, Benoliel says the South of France — with the exception of Marseille — hasn’t been as affected by the riots as big cities like Paris or Lille.

“When you watch what’s happening on television, you get an impression that doesn’t necessarily reflect the reality on the ground,” he says.

The violence also spooked crew members staying in Nice, where shops were looted over the weekend, says Isabelle Desgorges, a Gaumont executive whose team is handling production services on the “Ocean’s” prequel.

“My entire crew is staying in Nice, so there was a bit of panic, especially because it’s a big American movie. People were wondering what on earth was going on,” Desgorges says. “But fortunately, we weren’t filming on Saturday or Sunday, and our crew wasn’t directly caught up in the violence; they saw it from a distance. Still, it creates a strange atmosphere.”

The production began filming in Paris in late July before moving south to Monaco, where it is completing its shoot ahead of a few additional days filming at a water tank in Belgium.

Desgorges is worried the images of violence spreading on social media and news channels could temporarily give American producers cold feet about working in France for the time being.

“I wouldn’t go so far as to say that Americans no longer want to come to France. But inevitably, it’s going to create some tension for a few weeks,” she says. “It’s a good thing that this isn’t happening in July.”

The riots comes at a time when France has been enjoying a surge in international production activity, particularly in the South of France. Cannes alone had logged 310 filming days by early September, including work on “The White Lotus” and “Emily in Paris.”

The fallout is also being felt by France’s movie theaters, particularly in city centers where curfews have been introduced. Since Monday, Macron has ordered localized nighttime curfews in major cities, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Lille, Limoges and Bordeaux, among others.

Richard Patry, president of France’s National Federation of French Cinemas (FNCF), says “around 20 to 30 theaters are being affected by curfew measures,” but stresses France counts around 2,500 cinemas, which gives moviegoers plenty of alternatives.

“Clearly, there has been an impact, but it’s impossible to quantify. The only thing I can tell you is that the week ending Tuesday was up 12% compared with the equivalent week a year ago,” he says. “The cinemas that have been directly affected can calculate their losses by comparing their usual attendance with what they’re seeing now, but everywhere else, it’s virtually impossible.”

In Paris, the curfew is impacting the UGC Ciné Cité Les Halles, the sprawling Paris multiplex which ranks among the world’s busiest cinemas by admissions.

The multiplex has moved its last screening to 7 p.m. to allow moviegoers to return home before the curfew.

“Of course, it’s an extremely important movie theater, and closing earlier has an impact. Some people aren’t going there because of the curfew. That’s a reality,” Patry says.

Eric Marti at Rentrak France says the riots coincided with a drop of approximately 100,000 admissions on Saturday compared with the previous weekend, an especially disappointing result given that it marked the beginning of the school holidays. “We should have done better,” he says.

But moviegoing rebounded the following day, with Sunday admissions rising by 80,000 compared with the previous Sunday. “There was a catch-up effect,” Marti says.

Some of the big releases last week included Studiocanal’s “Les Miserables,” starring Vincent Lindon and Tahar Rahim, which had a slow opening weekend and managed to sell 480,822 tickets in its first week.

Overall admissions for the week ending Tuesday were actually up 12% compared with last year, while French box office has been up more than 26% since the beginning of 2026, per Patry.

“Despite everything that’s happening, despite how anxiety-inducing the situation is, people still want to go to the cinema. And they’re going,” he says.

For now, both exhibitors and producers are watching closely to see whether the violence will become a recurring problem in the run-up to the presidential election, with the far right and radical left parties leading in polls.

This weekend promises to be once more packed with action, with another day of nationwide protests slated for Saturday, this time in the presence of military forces. Yet, some major live events are going ahead as planned, notably the NFL’s first game in Paris between the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. A few days later, the Accor Arena, where Céline Dion performed, is still due to host Macklemore’s “Free Palestine” tour on Oct. 29.

And if there was any proof that live entertainment events could still thrive amid the chaos, it was Dion. Last Saturday, Dion was able to wrap the first leg of her comeback residency in the French capital and return to the five-star Royal Monceau hotel right by the Champs-Élysées avenue, where luxury boutiques including Louis Vuitton and Christian Dior had their windows smashed and merchandise stolen.

The Canadian superstar had also found herself unexpectedly drawn into France’s political debate after President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte attended her concert on the eve of the riots. Their social outing drew criticism in the French media as the presidential couple was accused of being tone-deaf, and were even compared to Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette on the eve of the French Revolution.

#474. ‘Apart,’ Set in Cyprus and Apartheid South Africa, “Challenges the Idea of ‘Us’ and ‘Them'” (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)

Writer-director Stelana Kliris’ feature, starring Leem Lubany and Luca Pasqualino and inspired by the experiences of her refugee parents, will open PÖFF’s Critics’ Picks section.

Can a young woman forced to leave a divided Cyprus in the 1970s find belonging and even love in an arranged marriage in Apartheid South Africa, especially when a secret from her past threatens to change everything? With Apart, South African Cypriot writer-director Stelana Kliris (Find Me Falling, Committed) has created a deeply personal film about displacement, belonging, borders, both the ones that are physical and those that are in our hearts, and human connections. And it is inspired by the real experiences of her refugee parents.

The movie, world-premiering at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), stars Leem Lubany (Omar, Rock the Kasbah), Luca Pasqualino (Rivals, The Musketeers) and Girley Jazama (Under the Hanging Tree, The White Line). Related Stories Movies 'Biermann' Director Explains Why His Doc About a German Political Singer Is a Film for the Trump Era Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title

“In 1974, when Turkey invades Cyprus, young Eleni (Lubany) leaves her homeland through an arranged marriage and finds herself in Apartheid South Africa, swapping one divided country for another,” reads a synopsis for the film. “There, a new life with Nico (Pasqualino) slowly turns into love, until an unexpected friendship forces her to confront a secret from her past.”

Shot in Cyprus with a story that goes between Cyprus and South Africa, Apart brings a turbulent time in the 1970s to life, with a focus on a female perspective. The filmmaker’s Find Me Falling became the first Cypriot film to premiere on Netflix.

Apart will open Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks section. “With this very personal and ambitious film, Stelana Kliris has delivered a deeply moving cinematic ode to humanity, a film that will stay with you long after the final frame,” the festival website teases.

With cinematography by Simon Sarketzis and editing by Emilios Avraam, Apart is being sold by Reinvent Yellow Sales. The producers are Kliris, Susan Simnett, Jamie Harvey and Ioanna Bolomyti.

“It has always fascinated me that people like my parents, who emigrated from Cyprus to South Africa, left one divided place for another, and I wanted to translate this into a film that challenges the idea of ‘us’ and ‘them,’ and, whilst the central narrative is fictional, the individual events around it are from real events,” Kliris says. “This is an intimate, character-driven film with a specific set of aesthetics that represents not just the two locations, but two distinct periods, 1970s South Africa interwoven with flashbacks to the Cypriot past, and while war and Apartheid serve as the backdrop, our story of love, friendship and identity provides for a more human, intimate experience.”

THR can now exclusively premiere the trailer for Apart. Prepare for a touching journey through time and across the globe to get a first glimpse of the challenges and emotions the protagonists experience.

#475. Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?

Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

#476. Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts

Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.

The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options.

"We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own."

The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.

While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.

The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices.

In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street.

Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.

Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period.

The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%.

Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits.

The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

#477. Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Severe sunburn increases the risk of developing melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer.Credit: Olga Pankova/Getty

A personalized mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of skin cancer returning or the recipient dying by 42% when used alongside an immunotherapy drug, according to long-awaited results for what could become the first approved mRNA vaccine for cancer.

Oncologists regard a risk reduction of 10% as substantial, says Kristen Radford, an immunotherapist at Mater Research in Brisbane. A more than 40% risk reduction “would send many researchers over the Moon”, adds Seth Cheetham, a geneticist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

The personalized vaccine, called intismeran, is not designed to prevent skin cancer, or melanoma, from developing in the first place, but to stop it returning in people who have already undergone surgery to remove tumours.

Anticipation for the trial results has been building since August, when the vaccine’s developers — Merck, based in Rahway, New Jersey, and Moderna, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts — announced early positive results. Data from the phase III trial will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on 24 October. But when data were leaked online on 22 October, the companies released the key results.

The stock price for Moderna, a pioneer in mRNA vaccine technology, had been rising since the August announcement, but dropped by around 25% after the leak. Health-care financial analyst Evan Seigerman at BMO Capital Markets in New York City told media company Forbes that such reactions in the stock market probably reflect “inflated expectation into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy”.

The intismeran trial enrolled 1,137 people with moderate to advanced melanoma across 157 centres. Participants were randomly assigned to receive a tailor made vaccine (intismeran) alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab — which is already used to treat melanoma — or pembrolizumab plus an inactive placebo. Trial leader Georgina Long, an oncologist at Melanoma Institute Australia in Sydney, says participants have so far been followed for around 25 months and will continue to be monitored for several years to determine whether the vaccine improves overall survival. She adds that the therapy did not result in any major harmful side effects.

Roughly 15 years ago, people with advanced melanoma typically survived for only months. Today, nearly 55% are effectively cured with targeted drugs or immunotherapies, says Long. The combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab is designed for people whose cancer could return after surgery and who do not respond to immunotherapy alone, she says.

Jessamy Tiffen, a cancer geneticist at the Centenary Institute in Sydney, says that the trial results are exciting, but only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years. “Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them,” she says. Furthermore, some people did not respond to the vaccine, she says.

Long says that her team will conduct a statistical analysis to identify who is most likely to benefit from the treatment.

To develop intismeran, Long and her colleagues sequenced DNA from a sample of each participant’s tumour to identify mutations in the cancer cells. These mutations can give rise to proteins called neoantigens, which help to distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones.

#479. ‘It’s the President’s Fault’: The White House Blame Game Starts Early Ahead of the Midterms

Trump White House aides have started to cast about for a scapegoat to offer the president in the event of bad midterm election losses, as Republicans stare down brutal predictions in key House and Senate races, sources familiar with the matter say.

Republican political operatives say privately that the real blame lies with Trump for starting the Iran war in an election year, causing higher prices across the board and prompting a nationwide voter backlash, the sources say.

“Clearly it's the president's fault,” one operative tells Inner Loop.

But Trump aides also know, for obvious reasons, they cannot say publicly or tell the president behind closed doors that his own policy decisions are at fault as they contemplate losing not just the House majority, but possibly the Senate.

The result has been an unusually early effort to find a scapegoat, and sources say eyes have fallen on deputy chief of staff and political strategist James Blair, who organized the Trump 2024 campaign's turnout strategy and returned to the role for this midterm cycle.

Blair's efforts included a marquee plan for certain states to redraw congressional maps early, which looked likely—though not certain—to yield favorable House seats for Republicans, so long as the coalition that Trump turned out in 2024 came out to support Republicans in 2026.

Even accounting for the Iran war, the redistricting gambit was supposed to bring roughly 10 to 15 pickups for Republicans in the House. After Virginia's top court blocked Democrats from redrawing maps to keep pace in the redistricting battle, Blair wrote on X: “Lord grant me humility.”

But in a remarkable backfire five months later, election forecasters have found that some of the redistricted seats now favor Democrats.

The redrawn map for Florida's 25th congressional district just south of Fort Lauderdale, for instance, is now characterized as "Lean Democrat," and the outlook is so bad that the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republican–aligned group, has pulled money out of the race.

Maps that were drawn for Republicans in ruby-red Texas are suddenly also vulnerable, even in seats where the party has incumbents. In Texas' 15th congressional district, GOP candidate Monica De La Cruz's race is now rated a "tossup" by the Cook Political Report.

Blair's allies inside and outside the West Wing say the criticism directed at him is grossly unfair because he could not have foreseen the effects of the Iran war and scandals involving Trump officials undoing his planning.

Blair is also viewed as retaining the confidence of Trump and the White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and he traveled on Air Force One to two rallies within the past week, suggesting any blame that ultimately comes his way could be just symbolic.

After all, when Blair left the White House earlier this year to run Trump's midterm strategy from the outside, the president announced the move as only temporary and said that Blair would return after the election.

Responding to the reporting in this story, Blair said in a statement, “the President, our partners in the House and Senate, and I remain focused on winning in November. All Republicans should be spending themselves equally in our worthy cause.”

“The anonymous ‘sources’ peddling this nonsense are self-serving opportunists focused on themselves. We’re focused on the President and the American people,” White House spokesperson Danielle Alvarez added in a statement.

As for Wiles herself, despite reporting that she has been under fire, sources inside Trump's orbit are adamant that if Wiles leaves after the midterms, it will be purely of her own volition.

Trump aides acknowledge that much of the palace intrigue scapegoating is preemptive. Expectations are so low that if Republicans take some wins—like holding on to the Senate—Blair will be “seen as a savior,” one of the sources added.

But they also say that in many ways Blair has perhaps made it too easy for them to single him out. He explicitly owned the House midterm strategy, and now he may be walked to the gallows with that same rope.

#480. Avatar: Seven Havens finally shows us how Korra broke the world

Since Avatar Studios announced Avatar: Seven Havens, Avatar fans' biggest question has been, "How did Avatar Korra cause the apocalypse?"

In Seven Havens episode 7, we finally get closer to finding out.

The episode continues twin Avatars Pavi (voiced by Saheli Khan) and Nisha's (voiced by Aishu Devan) quest to find their parents. Their investigation brings them back to the mysterious glowing red anomaly that has plagued Ellora on and off throughout the season. It left behind a mass of crystals following its resurgence in the zombie-influenced "Night of the Afflicted," and when Pavi and Nisha tunnel beneath those crystals, they discover the ruins of what appears to be an old world factory. Based on the gear logo on the wall and an old mover showing Asami Sato cutting a ribbon outside the building, it's a Futures Industries factory.

Want more film and TV news and reviews delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable’s Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Deep in the bowels of the factory, Pavi finds a vast pit full of a strange liquid whose surface ripples with the glowing red design of the anomaly. As she makes contact with it, she's greeted with a memory of Republic City before the Cataclysm. The city has been completely rebuilt following the battle with Kuvira at the end of The Legend of Korra, in which Korra created a new spirit portal within the city's Spirit Wilds. Now, the yellow beam of that portal appears to emerge straight from a Future Industries tower, suggesting that the people of Republic City have built over or around the Spirit Wilds. That couldn't possibly have a negative impact on the physical world's relationship with the Spirit World, right?

In Pavi's anomaly vision, she also sees a concerned-looking Korra, one who's much older than when we last left her, flying from Air Temple Island to Republic City. When Nisha joins Pavi in the vision, the scene changes drastically. The twins find themselves in the city streets, surrounded by fires and explosions. As the smoke clears from a motorcycle crash, the twins see Korra again. This time, though, she's changed: She's in the Avatar State, and she sports a menacing smirk. That can only mean one thing. The twins are seeing the moment Korra somehow turned and broke the world.

As Pavi and Nisha look on, Korra reaches up to pipe-like structures running along Republic City's skyscrapers and tears them down. The breaking of the pipes unleashes massive bands of destructive purple energy beams, which look very similar to the spirit vine energy Kuvira harnessed in her campaign to conquer Republic City.

That's all we get of the Cataclysm, but there's already a lot to unpack here, from Republic City's new look to the purple energy beams. Most fascinating of all might be the pipe structures Korra is tearing down. Their design is not rigid and pipe-like, but instead resembles vines. In rebuilding Republic City, could its citizens have tried to harness spirit energy from the Spirit Wilds as an energy source? Did they build around the vines climbing up buildings, and if so, did that strategy backfire spectacularly, contributing to the Cataclysm? Based on Republic City's skyline and these mysterious pipes, it seems like the physical world's relationship with the Spirit World was already way out of whack by the time the Cataclysm happened. That's odd, given that much of Korra's time as the Avatar was focused on maintaining that balance. After all, she opened the spirit portals at the poles and in Republic City.

That brings us to Korra herself. Let's be totally real here. That smirking woman in the Avatar State might look like Korra and bend like Korra, but that frightening smile and the intent on destroying the world just doesn't feel like her. Obviously, a lot has changed since we last saw Korra on TV, but I refuse to believe she had an entire personality transplant!

Instead, this version of Korra in the Avatar State recalls a more sinister figure from Book 2 in The Legend of Korra. In the climax of that season, villain Unalaq merged with the darkness spirit Vaatu to create a dark Avatar whose eyes glowed red, contrasting with the white glow of the light spirit Raava, who lives within the Avatar. In the Seven Havens vision, Korra's eyes still glow white, yet her unsettling body language screams that the Avatar State has been corrupted in some way.

By the end of Season 2, Korra defeated Vaatu, but did not destroy him outright. Instead, his spirit is set to regrow within Raava over a period of 10,000 years, until the next Harmonic Convergence. That's a ways off within the Avatar timeline, but could the rapid acceleration of technology or Korra's proximity to the Spirit Wilds have accelerated that growth somewhat? Or alternatively, did some Future Industries technology create the anomaly and trigger some dark turn in Korra? I could very well be barking up the wrong spirit vine, but I have a feeling Book 2 of The Legend of Korra is about to become very, very important.

Clearly, we haven't gotten the full story yet, and Seven Havens is being very careful in how it doles out Korra's memories. In this episode alone, it leaves a gap between Korra's flight to Republic City and the Cataclysm. (Assuming the visions happen on the same night, that is, as Korra is wearing the exact same outfit in both.) That gap could be key to understanding Korra's motives in bringing on the Cataclysm, and hopefully in clearing her name somewhat in the timeline of Seven Havens.

#481. ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Review: Masculinity and Its Constructs Are Explored in a Revealing Docu-Fiction Study of Egyptian Bodybuilders

Muhammad Mustapha’s quest to understand his fascination with exaggerated muscle mass takes him on a 10-year journey of self-examination.

How else can we explain why some men torture their bodies into unnatural shapes, other than a terror of powerlessness? The men in Mustapha’s docu-fiction hybrid are all working-class guys whose outsized bodies allow them to instill fear in everyone whose dominance is of the less physical kind. Yet to undergo the kind of pain they embrace, to willingly become slaves of their own steroid-plumped bodies, takes the concept to another dimension. “Big Boys” doesn’t attempt to hide the director’s ambivalent gaze, mesmerized by the sheer mass of deltoids and triceps whose exaggerated size borders on the cartoonish. Instead, Mustapha seeks to understand his own fascination with (literally) inflated forms of masculinity, which led him on this 10-year journey with bodybuilders whose aura of menace isn’t always undercut by hoped-for revelations of sensitivity. Popular on Variety

He opens with a montage of men training for fights, explaining in voiceover how he’s always wanted to shoot a fight scene but the camera failed to get to underneath the strange dance between softness and violence. Instead, he could only capture the performance, disappointed at how his view remained on the surface. The irony is that, by the film’s end, surface remains the most tangible element, unsurprising given that bodybuilding is by its very nature a theatrical construct whose visual impact is far more coherent than can be verbalized by the majority of its practitioners. On that level, Denis Côté’s “A Skin So Soft” was more accepting of the fascination offered by exteriors alone.

Though not addressed in the film, masculinity in Egypt was already a performative fabrication in the late 19th century, as discussed in Wilson Chacko Jacob’s trailblazing book “Working Out Egypt,” when so-called “effendi masculinity” sought to counter notions of colonial subjugation by emphasizing strength and the assertion of an at-times exaggerated concept of maleness. The bodybuilders in Mustapha’s focus are the inheritors of that model, using their Hulk-like muscles to exert temporary power over homegrown overlords who keep them in a kind of class subjugation. In this iteration, their physiques are displayed not for aesthetic purposes but as a visual manifestation of volatile power.

Abdullah Al-Araby, the main subject, is in many ways the perfect embodiment of this notion. Working as a bouncer (like many of his fellow bodybuilders) when not in the gym, Abdullah was in jail at one point — the film’s timeline can be frustratingly unclear — and remains invested in cultivating a menacing aura that’s marketable for those wanting to shake down associates. Unsurprisingly, when Abdullah and his friends are asked what roles they’d like to play if they turned to acting, all of them choose villains and mob bosses.

While “Perform” is the title assigned the film’s first chapter, in reality the term could be used throughout. “Construct” comes next, revealing the grueling effort it takes to maintain bodies of unnatural proportions. (A cupping scene accompanied by blood-letting is not for the squeamish.) Here, “no pain, no gain” is taken to its most extreme, where even the performance of pain, exemplified by the grimaces bodybuilders make in competitions where they distort not just their physiques but their expressions, underlines the notion that masculinity and agony go hand-in-hand.

At the end of the day, for all of Mustapha’s claims of friendship, the truth is his relationship with Abdullah cannot be an even one: the director is from the educated classes, able to move in and out of this world, whereas his subject is as trapped in his social status as he is in his body. A scene in which Abdullah practically tortures his very young sons for not pushing themselves harder becomes one of the film’s most revealing moments, even more so than the final shot where the two men are on a motorbike, their banter unwittingly revealing the insurmountable gap between them.

“Big Boys” would have benefited from a little more explanation: we know several scenes are staged, but their purpose can feel forced, and Mustapha’s fascination with these oversized exemplars of synthetic masculinity, stemming from his identification as a “sensitive” man, perhaps doesn’t go quite far enough. Largely devoid of homoeroticism (this is contemporary Egypt, after all), the film is unable to resolve its own conundrum: Are these exaggerated muscles attractive or repellent? And more importantly, what is this anxiety so many men feel about their emotions that drives them to torturously invent bodies that bear little resemblance to the human form?

#482. ‘Biermann’ Director Explains Why His Doc About a German Political Singer Is a Film for the Trump Era

Jens Meurer discusses his doc, screening at Austria's Viennale and showing Wolf Biermann narrating his life in various iterations of Germany, and how the outspoken artist inspired 'The Lives of Others.'

Biermann, the new documentary film from Jens Meurer (An Impossible Project, Public Enemy, Seaside Special), is a portrait of the outspoken political singer-songwriter and poet Wolf Biermann. Through the lens of his life, though, it also offers a cinematic reflection on the 20th-century history of Germany, Europe and the world. After all, Biermann has lived in five different versions of Germany.

Born in Hamburg in 1936, Biermann only met his father once – in prison before the Jewish communist was killed by the Nazis in Auschwitz. The doc shows how this experience gave Biermann his calling: to fight against injustice and for socialism. He moved to East Germany and made a name for himself as a critical and fearless voice in the GDR. To some, Biermann, who is still a close friend of Joan Baez’s, was like an East German Bob Dylan. The GDR regime banned him, forcing him to perform for 12 years in his East Berlin living room. When he played a concert in Cologne, West Germany, in 1976 in front of 7,500 people, the regime banned Biermann again – this time from re-entering East Germany. That saw the political artist live in exile in West Germany until he could visit the Eastern part of Germany again after reunification. Related Stories Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title TV 'MobLand' EP Teases What Season 3 Holds for Tom Hardy as 'Laird' Star Peter Sarsgaard Shares How He Feels About Playing a "Malevolent U.S. Billionaire"

Shot on 16mm film, Biermann follows the critical voice and father of 10 children as he narrates his David-versus-Goliath life, going through his everyday life, to performances and visiting to historic locations. It also features interviews with his contemporaries, including actor Armin Mueller-Stahl, who lauds his fire of rebellion but also calls him a “visible egomaniac,” and archive footage.

Biermann screens at the 64th edition of the Viennale, the Vienna film festival in Austria, which runs through Nov. 3, on Oct. 26 and Oct. 27, following its recent FilmFest Hamburg world premiere. Majestic Filmverleih will release the film in Germany, with Filmladen releasing it in Austria.

The Instant Film, Zeitsprung Pictures, Clouds Hill and zero fiction production was written by Dirk Kämper, Meurer and Biermann’s wife Pamela Biermann, who also appears in the film. Sebastian Ganschow and Bernd Fischer handled cinematography, with editing by Antje Lass, Zenon Kristen and Grete Jentzen.

Meurer talked to THR about how Biermann’s story relates to the Oscar-winning movie The Lives of Others, its timeliness in the age of Trump and why the songwriter’s messages are universal.

Wolf Biermann is well known in Germany, and his work is in German. But his story and work feel quite universal. What’s your take?

Yes, there is even an obvious Biermann pitch for an international audience, namely that the premise of The Lives of Others is based on his situation. It’s not his story, but Biermann’s apartment was the most observed apartment by the Stasi secret police in East Germany.

The original impetus for the film, to be honest, was to look at an incredible life story over a long German period. But as we got into the film, it became clearer and clearer that this is a film for today and about today. Biermann might turn 90 in two weeks, but he’s speaking to us very much also about the situation today.

I firmly believe this isn’t just a German story. At the very least, this is a European story, but it’s really a story for all of us in the world. It’s a story of somebody who stood up to power, who managed to speak his mind, express his opposition and speak for freedom, no matter what. And he did so not just in a brave manner, but also in a very humorous manner.

If I look at Trump, I think, “Where’s Charlie Chaplin!?” We should not be cowed. We should be making fun of these people, and that was Biermann’s biggest secret weapon – he attacked the dictatorship that he lived under with passion and humor. It’s an entertaining film – lots of laughter.

There is a scene in the film where Biermann goes back to East Germany after the fall of the wall and tells people that they didn’t speak out against the GDR regime enough, which underlines that what he tells us can be quite uncomfortable.

Yeah, he’s a real character. He gets a lot of resistance because he’s abrasive and doesn’t mince his words. He is – maybe that word is overused – authentic. It’s the kind of authenticity that we badly, badly need these days. And in that sense, he’s a secret weapon, and not just in Germany.

But what’s interesting is that he touches both people of his and my generation, but also young people who may not have heard his name before, but he speaks to them even more. I think there’s a thirst for that uprightness. His most famous song is called “Ermutigung,” or “Encouragement.” I think it’s what people are longing for and you get that with him, as you see in the film.

In the film, we see a woman mention that people have sometimes called Biermann the “Bob Dylan of Germany”…

The quote you’re referring to is really from the 1970s and from writer Barbara Honigmann, who said that for East Germans, he was their Bob Dylan. What she really means is that he was a figurehead; he was a leader in writing songs that spoke for people, that were original and that found words in a way that Bob Dylan did. They spoke to their generation; in Biermann’s case, the generation of opposition to this gray, boring and really terrible Stalinist dictatorship that they were living under.

Did you and Biermann know each other before you started work on the film? And how long did you film him?

No, it was a bit of a blind date. Somebody arranged for us to meet who thought there had been no documentary about him since 1982. There have been lots of TV interviews, but not a documentary. And somebody thought maybe these two would get along. We were introduced and hit it off very quickly. It was amazing to discover how much life there is in this 90-year-old.

We also hit it off because my approach is different. I shoot on film, and I do not do that for retro reasons or because it looks better or something like that. It’s the tool that I use to very respectfully, but veryrespectfully intrusively, get into people’s lives in a way so that we all enjoy the process. It’s very above board because you can’t hide a film camera, but it focuses everyone. That’s something that Biermann really appreciated. So, we filmed over the course of two years, and that led to a lot of time spent together, with and without camera. You have to choose your moments, working on film.

What was the most difficult thing about making Biermann?

The hardest part is that this is a 90-year-old German whose life [covers] a German century. He’s a Holocaust survivor who’s still a public and political force today. He’s currently on concert tour, filling large halls, for God’s sake! He’s somebody who’s had an incredible lifespan as a musician and as a poet. Biermann is actually Germany’s most published poet in the German language since World War II, and he’s still writing songs now.

He’s also on a concert tour, playing three-and-a-half-hour concerts this week. So, he’s still top fit. He is just a really great pianist, but he’s famous as a songwriter on the guitar.

For me, the film was also a discovery of his Jewish roots and of his communist roots all the way to the great role he played in changing German history with this expulsion from East Germany. He has lived in five Germanys. He grew up in Nazi Germany, lived in post-war occupied Germany, and then West Germany. He also moved to and lived in East Germany, and then [was sent back to West Germany] and now has been living in the reunited Germany. So one life, five Germanys.

There is no more German, European or world story in one person than his. If anyone thinks that this is just a German story, I think that’s a huge misunderstanding. This is such a larger-than-life, true-life story, and it’s such a universal message embodied in this extraordinary person.

Is there any particular inspiration that you feel Biermann and the man it is about can provide?

The man is 90, and he’s been through a lot, including having seen his father once in his life before he was murdered in Auschwitz. But he is still exuding a kind of optimism in spite of the shit show we are making our world into at the moment.

Something that I really want to capture in the documentaries I am making is this optimism. There’s plenty of room for films that tell the stories of all the challenges and woes that we are facing. Weirdly enough, it seems that there isn’t a big market for a film that also shows that maybe there is something positive in us, some agency. There’s definitely something in Biermann that also gives us cause for confidence that we are able to stand up, that each of us is able to do something. Biermann has a great line: Get fucking involved in your own life and in your own matters.

Just think of the David-versus-Goliath story of his life. He is a brilliant poet and songwriter but banned for 12 years. He couldn’t perform or be published in his own country for 12 years. So, he just recorded secretly, and his music was smuggled out into the West. So he was banned in East Germany but a best-selling musician in the West.

I think one great moment in the film is when he talks about his old apartment, and outside of it, there were all these trams, and they couldn’t edit them out of the recordings. So he just embraced them and said, “Those trams are my musicians.” And in West Germany, when people listened to these records, they said, “Oh man, that’s the great authentic sound of the East.”

I just started on a sequel of sorts to my film An Impossible Project. But this time around, it’s a “possible” project. It originates with the same [analogue enthusiast] character from Vienna, “Doc” [Florian Kaps], the guy who saved the last Polaroid factory in the world, against all odds.

He also got involved in saving vinyl, and he’s recently teamed up, after years and years of not really getting it right, to invent a new kind of vinyl recording machine. He teamed up with a totally fascinating Swedish company called Teenage Engineering. Together, they want to fight back and conquer America in a good way with a different kind of approach to what technology can be, namely that technology can also empower us as people, and not just enslave us.

#483. Trump Isn’t Even Good at TV Anymore

Once upon a time, Donald Trump’s talents as a TV personality and pitchman were obvious to everyone—most of all himself.

When he launched his 2016 presidential run, millions of Americans knew him best not from his bankrupt casinos or the gossip pages of the New York Post but as the swaggering host of NBC’s The Apprentice, in which aspiring entrepreneurs competed for a full-time job in his real estate empire.

Trump routinely overstated the primetime dominance of The Apprentice, which was a breakout hit in its debut 2003–2004 season but saw its ratings steadily decline over subsequent years. Nonetheless, his rise as a candidate, propelled by his willingness to say anything to stay in the news cycle, seemed to affirm his on-camera star quality (even if it was actually people behind the scenes of The Apprentice who had edited his unscripted and less-than-coherent bluster to make him sound like a straight-talking businessman).

But where is Trump’s TV firepower today? His latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, lasted a mere five days in the job, ousted following a disastrous on-camera performance at her first briefing just weeks before crucial midterm elections. Trump’s own media appearances are unhinged and embarrassing even by his standards; when he’s not falling asleep at events or in meetings, he’s claiming that NATO “gave” Greenland to the US and telling rallygoers about how he checked out Senator Jon Husted’s ass.

During Trump’s second term, his administration has done what it can to circumvent existing media and bring its messaging directly to voters with broadcast content that resembles familiar TV formats. It’s not breaking through at all.

On Tuesday, for example, the US Small Business Administration streamed an hour-long special called the Million Dollar Pitch Competition. The premise was that five business owners would appear before three celebrity judges (property investor Grant Cardone, rapper Nicki Minaj, and Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia, whose credentials as a member of Elon Musk’s DOGE were not mentioned) to vie for the biggest chunk of a $1 million cash prize supplied by Clover Network, a fintech company that provides point-of-sale platforms.

While the show, hosted by actor Dean Cain, was styled as something like a hybrid of Shark Tank and American Idol, it amounted to an extraordinarily dull attempt to prove that the Trump administration is bringing factory jobs back to the US. For some reason, it featured a short video in which Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, talked to an animated strand of DNA, because “America's DNA is small business.” The judges focused more on how animated the presenters were than the economic fundamentals of their pitch. When Marshall Sasse, the owner and CEO of a pressure valve company based in Wyoming, delivered a solid but subdued presentation, Minaj asked if he had access to any “cowgirls” who could’ve added “more punch to the pitch.”

While Trump himself was not on hand for the pitches, the show featured brief segments in which participants met with Trump in the Oval Office. When the judges asked the president for advice on picking a winner, Trump replied, “You know, it's interesting, because with The Apprentice, I had a very good term that I used: ‘You're fired.’”

A day later, the YouTube stream of the SBA’s Million Dollar Pitch Competition had barely cracked 60,000 views. Even on Trump-friendly X, the reaction to the event was hostile, with users suggesting that the White House cared more about game shows than the cost of living and was taking its cues from dystopian fiction such as The Hunger Games.

Other efforts to supplant mainstream programming have also fared poorly. A month after the White House launched a 24/7 Trump TV streaming channel as part of its ongoing war on news outlets, it’s hard to imagine even the most devoted MAGA disciple watching: on Tuesday, unremarkable B-roll footage from border agents driving alongside the US-Mexico wall segued into a series of testimonials from people describing how their loved ones were raped and murdered by migrants. On Wednesday, the channel showed footage from Trump’s February State of the Union address.

As for Robert F. Kennedy’s The Real Food Show on YouTube, a cooking series in which the health secretary enlists chefs to teach viewers affordable and healthy home recipes, audience has declined since a July premiere, with only six episodes released so far. The most recent segment included Cain as well as actor and ex-bodybuilder Lou Ferrigno, as though to underscore that on the celebrity front, some of Trump world’s biggest names are guys known for playing superheroes on TV in the previous century.

If there has been any sort of a ratings win for MAGA media this year, it would be UFC Freedom 250, the mixed martial arts extravaganza held in June at a ring structure controversially erected on the South Lawn of the White House. Though Ultimate Fighting Championship lost some $30 million on the spectacle, it broke the viewership record for a live event airing exclusively on streamer Paramount+, with an average of 7 million viewers tuned in.

That fell well short of the Super Bowl records that Dana White, CEO of UFC, had promised to break. While he was nonetheless able to declare a victory for his sports organization, White has said that he “can’t afford” to return to Trump’s backyard for an encore. Too bad for the administration, which has yet to capture a real TV audience without significant help from a producer who knows what they’re doing.

#484. General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance

DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.

The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.

Despite the positive news, GM stock fell nearly 7% during trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations.

Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG.

Several analysts in investor notes Tuesday said GM's third-quarter results were solid, but raised concerns about whether higher costs and pressures on vehicle pricing would limit earnings growth next year.

Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

GM's new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.

That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.

"I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau. "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."

GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries.

While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.

Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal.

"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.

The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.

The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.

GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.

GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

#485. How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?

Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

Will sustainability become a core principle or an afterthought?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

David Zamora is the chairman of the Space Data Association. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights.

The commercialization of space is well underway, and as a result, Earth’s orbit is becoming ever more congested. The current number of active satellites in orbit stands at around 16,000, according to the European Space Agency( ESA), and this number is expected to jump close to 60,000 by 2035, Novaspace projects. While it’s not always given the recognition it deserves, space has fast become a critical infrastructure layer, underpinning nearly all systems that enable modern life as we know it. Therefore, it’s critical that a safe and clean operating landscape is maintained.

Yet this is becoming increasingly challenging, particularly given that, alongside the rapid increase in space traffic, there are also more than 1.2 million pieces of debris over 1 centimeter (0.4 inches) cm in Earth’s orbit, each of which could damage satellites and spacecraft and potentially cause disastrous consequences. With the number of active satellites and debris objects in space continuing to increase, the space environment is under growing pressure.

Space was once the sole domain of nation states, but this is no longer the case. As technology has advanced, launch costs have decreased, and satellites have become more efficient, smaller and cheaper to build. These changes have democratized space, resulting in a massive increase in space traffic, not least constellations in low Earth orbit (LEO) that comprise thousands of satellites.

Plans are underway to further expand these constellations, and new and even bigger constellations are also expected to launch in the coming years. Added to that, we’re also likely to see the first space-based data centers within the next few years, which may well mark the start of the wholesale shift of data centers from Earth to space, which will further add to the congestion already being felt.

To ensure that space continues to meet our current and future needs, this continued expansion must happen in a sustainable way. Maintaining a safe and clean landscape is more important than ever before, and mitigating the impact of space debris is critical to that effort.

Mitigating the impact of debris involves a multipronged approach. Whether intentional or unintentional, the creation of new space debris by future space missions must be minimized as much as possible. This applies during launch, operation, and end of life phases, and satellites and other spacecraft need to be designed with this in mind. Additionally, satellites that are no longer active should not remain in orbit for extended periods, because this only increases the chance of collision events which would create new debris. The standard rule has been 25 years, but there are recommendations now that this should be lowered to five years.

Also critical is the prevention of in-orbit collisions between active satellites and other objects. This is only achievable through effective Space Situational Awareness (SSA) and Space Traffic Coordination (STC) systems. SSA maps out and characterizes objects in space (both satellites and debris), determining their location, trajectory and velocity, while STC actively manages the space traffic identified through SSA to prevent collisions. When a conjunction is probable, SSA/STC service providers alert the operators involved, who then decide whether to undertake a collision-avoidance maneuver.

Extending the operational life of satellites is another important aspect of debris mitigation because it reduces the need for so many new launches, thereby reducing the likelihood of more debris being created. Innovations such as electric propulsion systems that allow for greater maneuverability and extended mission durations are part of the solution, as is in-orbit servicing, maintenance and refuelling.

While these strategies focus on preventing new debris from being created, we also need effective methods for removing existing pieces of debris. This is a rapidly growing sector attracting much investment. Debris-removal technology being developed ranges from physical capture and tethered deorbit to destruction with ground and space-based laser ablation and plasma systems, as well as the emerging concept of mining debris to extract metals and gases for in-orbit processing to feed into the circular space economy.

The UN views space safety and space sustainability as urgent priorities. Its treaties and agreements focus on preserving the peaceful, safe, and sustainable use of outer space, preventing collisions, managing space debris, and ensuring responsible operations. Governments, space agencies and international organizations are also strengthening their focus on space sustainability.

ESA has launched its Zero Debris strategy, which is aimed at achieving a debris-neutral orbital environment by 2030. As part of this approach, ESA has updated its debris mitigation requirements and standards that will govern how its missions are designed, built, flown and disposed of. It also sets requirements for any company or institution that works with ESA on its missions.

In the U.K., the UK Space Agency is also taking a proactive role in space safety and sustainability through its Active Debris Removal (ADR) program and through the development of space sustainability standards in partnership with industry. It is also in the process of developing a space sustainability strategy to ensure a coordinated approach to sustainable practices in space.

On the other side of the pond, NASA’s Space Sustainability Strategy identifies five key challenges that are felt nationally but also within the wider space community. These include the absence of a single framework for space sustainability that has been accepted by the space community and the fact that space sustainability may be in tension with other mission interests. The strategy defines six goals that are intended to address each of the challenges alongside corresponding objectives to guide NASA’s achievements of the goals.

The U.S. is also building on the National Orbital Debris Mitigation Plan, which was released in 2022, with the Orbital Sustainability (ORBITS) Act. The Act, which has been introduced to the Senate but not yet been enacted into law, seeks to establish a program for the active remediation of orbital debris as well as requiring the development of uniform orbital debris standard practices. The Office of Space Commerce has also developed TraCSS (Traffic Coordination System for Space) to provide basic SSA data and services to civil and private space operators in support of spaceflight safety, although the system is currently in beta mode.

The International Standard Organisation (ISO) is also working on a standard for STC (Space Traffic Coordination) so that SSA activities can be standardized. Titled Space Systems — Space Traffic Coordination (STC), the standard is moving toward final publication, and its core focus is on establishing baseline protocols, data exchange formats and operational requirements for space safety, on-orbit conjunction assessment and collision avoidance.

While these strategies are certainly moving the industry in the right direction, there is a real need to act quickly. Success will rely not only on speed, but also on sustained and collaborative effort, as well as engagement from all space users. The decisions made and actions undertaken over the next decade will shape the space environment for generations to come.

As to whether sustainability becomes a core principle rather than an afterthought, that remains to be seen. There is, however, reason to be optimistic.

David Zamora is currently the Head of Flight Dynamics at Eutelsat. In this role, he is in charge of the overall management and organization of all flight dynamics (FD) related activities for the whole set of satellites controlled from the Eutelsat satellite control center in Paris, including: FD operations from beginning of life until satellite decommissioning, satellite collision avoidance and coordination of the specification of Flight Dynamics facilities. David has over 15 years’ experience in the space industry and he has led for Eutelsat the FD activities in the LEOP preparation (as FD Project Manager) and operations (as FD Director and Manager) for 6 Eutelsat satellites from two different satellite manufacturers.

#487. Yaga isnt the show Hudson Williams fans want it to be

There's so much to want to love in Canadian series Yaga, from its small-town mystery to its hints of folklore and witchcraft. But the biggest draw of all is undoubtedly its cast, which includes Carrie-Anne Moss, Noah Reid, Clark Backo, and Heated Rivalry breakout Hudson Williams.

Yaga is Williams' first major project to come out since the runaway success of Heated Rivalry catapulted him and co-star Connor Storrie to stardom. With that comes an opportunity for Williams to further showcase his range beyond his Canadian Screen Award-winning work as Shane Hollander. It's a shame, then, that Yaga gives Williams and his co-stars so little to latch onto, in a dark feminist fable that feels more hollow than revelatory.

Want more film and TV news and reviews delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable’s Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Based on the play by Kat Sandler, who also serves as showrunner, Yaga invites us to the small town of Whittock, where Henry Park (Williams), heir to a powerful fishery owner, has gone missing. Enter private investigator Rapp (Reid) and local police detective Carson (Backo), who are paired — reluctantly, on Carson's end — to get to the bottom of this mystery.

What begins as a standard missing persons investigation soon becomes something darker and stranger. Chicken carcasses hang menacingly on doors. Bloody symbols mar crime scenes. Through it all, Rapp hears whispers of Baba Yaga, a legendary witch from Slavic folklore known for living in a house on chicken legs and flying around in a mortar and pestle. Could Henry's disappearance be tied to the occult? Given that the whole series opens with images of an unknown figure being burned at the stake, and that each episode opens and closes with a voiceover monologue from a wizened witchy figure, the answer appears to be an unequivocal "yes."

So the stage is set for a strange, folkloric mystery. Yet Yaga's witchiness never truly sings. Too often, the show resorts to the same style of surreal fakeout dream sequences, where a stream of bloody feathers and foreboding masks blends into a shorthand for horror without truly scaring. The voiceovers, presented as coming from Baba Yaga herself, offer up platitudes about women who have been othered as witches, but they feel familiar to anyone who's ever read a "we are the granddaughters of the witches you couldn't burn" bumper sticker.

At the center of this witchy vortex is Williams' Henry, who mostly haunts Rapp and Carson's investigation in flashbacks, including a steamy podcast recording with him and intriguing professor Katherine (Moss), an expert in all things bone. Henry's not alone: Williams also plays Logan, Henry's roommate, podcasting partner, and doppelganger. (Yaga sticks Williams in a prosthetic nose and fake acne for the Logan role, and the result is a jarring trip to the uncanny valley.)

A dual role should be rich territory for any actor to mine, yet neither Henry nor Logan get enough screen time for Williams' double turn to truly sink in. Henry is primarily a confident, if sleazy, charmer, while Logan is mostly presented as an awkward, almost wooden foil to that charm. Logan was not a character in the original stage play, and it shows in his thinness here.

Yaga introduces a fascinating thread about Logan perhaps wanting to be (or maybe be with) Henry, but it rarely pulls it beyond the occasional unsettling sex scene. While onscreen intimacy can often be a great showcase of character dynamics, here, these scenes are often over too fast or accompanied by a voiceover that explains said dynamics without letting the actual performances breathe.

As Yaga unfurls, Henry and Logan become much more sinister figures. While the thought of Williams taking a villainous turn is an exciting one, his Henry and Logan don't make particularly compelling villains because we know so little of them. Yaga's leads don't tend to fare much better. Moss is slippery fun as Katherine, but too often she remains on the margins. Backo and Reid's buddy cop dynamic is punchy, yet often dragged down by Rapp's incessant flirting. That most of the women in Whittock practically throw themselves at him is one of Yaga's most infuriating features. As it happens again and again and again, these women's advances bypass sexual empowerment and move straight into bewilderment.

Yaga gestures out to interesting concepts, but ultimately, it never dives deep enough. As an examination of witchcraft as a conduit for female rage, it's not angry enough. As an erotic thriller, it's not titillating enough. As a mystery, its twists and turns are intriguing, but never quite captivating. The ingredients for success are there, but they never quite come together to cast the right spell.
