#562. Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes?

Bruno Fernandes has scored 111 goals in 338 appearances for Manchester United

Michael Carrick is never short of advice around how he should do his job as head coach of Manchester United.

Few of his players divide opinion quite so much as skipper Bruno Fernandes.

So, it stands to reason there are a variety of views around whether Fernandes should be dropped for Sunday's vital Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Former Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson has no doubts.

"It is a big problem for Michael," he told The Overlap podcast. "Put people in the team you trust. Your captain has thrown you under the bus. If you don't think he is playing for you, get him out. I wouldn't pick him even though he is their best player."

Joe Smith, respected host of Manchester United fan channel Stretford Paddock, is of the same opinion.

"I don't think Fernandes should play on the weekend," he said. "I don't think (Lisandro) MartÃ­nez should've played against Leeds, because otherwise they're running the ship here."

United fans heading back on flights from Como to Manchester had a view, although much of it was wrapped up in their general thoughts about the club, most of which were negative.

But only one man's opinion really counts. Carrick is the man who picks the team.

His friend and former team-mate Wayne Rooney has a view on that.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," he said on the United Stand podcast.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"I was in that situation [as manager at Plymouth and Birmingham City] and if I was in Carrick's position now, I'd come out fighting. There's no more Mr Nice Guy."

Fernandes was replaced by Joshua Zirkzee after 67 minutes of Manchester United's Champions League defeat in Como

Carrick is due to speak in a news conference to preview the Bournemouth game at 1330 BST.

He will be asked whether Bruno Fernandes is going to be dropped.

Many observers were shocked to discover Fernandes was not going to be disciplined for his post-match outburst following the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como. They were also surprised that he would remain as Manchester United skipper, when team-mate Lisandro Martinez was fined for attacking the club hierarchy eight days earlier after the 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid.

"It was an assassination," one source who has worked with Fernandes previously, told BBC Sport of Wednesday's comments.

"It was unprofessional. Michael's team are killing him."

The issue is whether Fernandes went too far in attacking Carrick's tactics for the Como game, then saying it was on the coaching team on the sidelines to spot the problem and change it, not the players.

Fernandes is one of the most knowledgeable members of Carrick's squad when it comes to football tactics, and is desperate to succeed. His comments, made on TNT Sports weren't off the cuff, or said in an emotional state after a defeat, as Lisandro Martinez's were.

Yet there is also sympathy for Fernandes from some at Old Trafford given the 32-year-old carried out 10 post-match interviews after the Como debacle, and also because, while hardly offering a defence of Carrick, the words were less inflammatory when they were spoken as they seem in text form.

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick apologised to the club's 700 travelling supporters for the 4-1 defeat at Como

It is easy to point to Sir Alex Ferguson, the former Manchester United manager who was a strong advocate of managers needing to have control over their players and wonder how he would have reacted to such a situation. Challenges to his authority tended to end with players leaving the club.

However, you only need to listen to Gordon Strachan recounting instances from Ferguson's time in charge at Aberdeen on 'The Good, The Bad and the Football podcast' to accept some of the Scot's more extreme methods would not be acceptable in the current climate.

United's hierarchy are keen to get away from the cycle of sacking managers, having dismissed Ruben Amorim last season and Erik ten Hag in the one before.

However, there is also a basic truth that Carrick desperately needs to end the present run of seven games without a win. If they fail against Bournemouth it would equal the sorry run of Louis van Gaal in 2015-16, which was the worst since a Ferguson-led side had eight draws and a defeat during the 1988-89 season.

So, with Benjamin Sesko, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford all ruled out through injury, can Carrick drop Fernandes even if he wanted to?

The Portuguese's link-up with Youri Tielemans has not flourished as imagined.

And the only goal contributions by last season's PFA player of the year have been a hat-trick and assist in the 5-2 win over Ipswich in August and his strike against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK on 10 September.

But, as Duncan Ferguson said, he is their best player. Carrick has to make the call. He needs to get it right.

#563. Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama

Empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change: Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement that has become the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years.

The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.

She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.

"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."

University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.

Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution." The protests began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.

The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.

Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.

A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.

The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down. They say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.

"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.

During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.

Then, at 8:03 a.m. local time on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.

"These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.

Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.

The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.

The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the EU. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.

Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"

For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.

"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," Xhemollari told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.

But the anger is not directed at Rama's administration alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.

"We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.

For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.

"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.

But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.

"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."

Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.

"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.

Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

#564. Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe

The largest collection of exploding white dwarf stars ever compiled is providing fresh evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force responsible for the Universe’s accelerating expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a central assumption of modern cosmology and could help scientists better understand how the Universe evolves.

An international research team led by scientists at the University of Queensland’s School of Mathematics and Physics brought together observations of 2,884 Type Ia supernovae. These powerful stellar explosions serve as important tools for measuring distances across the Universe, allowing astronomers to trace its expansion history.

PhD candidate Ryan Camilleri said the project establishes a new international standard for supernova cosmology. By bringing decades of measurements into a unified dataset, researchers have created their most detailed picture yet of how cosmic expansion has changed over time.

“We’ve rebuilt 3 decades of astronomical observations into a single, consistent framework,” Mr. Camilleri said.

“We combined our data with other cosmic measurements including relic light from the Big Bang and maps of how galaxies are distributed through space.

“Instead of confirming the standard model of cosmology which assumes dark energy is fixed and unchanging, we have more evidence that dark energy may change over time.”

The new collection brings together historical supernova measurements and findings from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) published in 2024.

To make observations collected over different periods directly comparable, the scientists revisited older data using updated analytical methods. Advances in understanding supernova behavior allowed the team to improve the consistency and accuracy of measurements gathered over decades.

“Over the years we’ve learned a lot more about how supernovae behave so we’ve been able to go back and apply that improved understanding to older data,” Mr. Camilleri said.

The researchers also had to account for differences among the telescopes used to collect the observations. Other factors, including cosmic dust and the masses of galaxies, can influence the light astronomers receive from distant supernovae and therefore affect distance measurements.

“Extensive work has been done to link observations from different telescopes with different capacities and take into account issues such as cosmic dust and galaxy mass which can affect the light coming from a supernova.

“We also incorporated more subtle effects such as gravitational lensing, which is the bending and magnification of light around large objects as it travels from a supernova to Earth.”

Astrophysicist Professor Tamara Davis said the expanded dataset represents an important advance in efforts to understand the nature of dark energy.

Under the standard model of cosmology, dark energy is treated as a constant property of the Universe. However, recent observations have raised questions about whether that assumption fully explains how cosmic expansion has evolved.

“Our supernova data from DES in 2024 first showed hints that dark energy may be time varying, and this new compilation also sees a deviation from the standard model although in a slightly different direction,” Professor Davis said.

The findings are especially interesting because a separate astronomical project has also produced evidence suggesting that dark energy might not remain constant.

“Similarly results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) found hints of variations in dark energy in its surveys of relic sound waves from the early Universe.

“So, 2 completely independent measurements have found hints of time variation in dark energy, challenging the standard model that dark energy doesn't change.

Although the different measurements do not point to exactly the same departure from the standard model, they provide additional reasons to investigate whether dark energy changes as the Universe ages.

Understanding dark energy could have implications extending far beyond the expansion of the Universe. Researchers believe that learning more about its behavior might also provide insights into one of the greatest unresolved problems in theoretical physics: reconciling gravity with quantum physics.

“All of this research may also hold the clue to explain how gravity and quantum physics fit together.

“We know these 2 theories are each immensely successful in their own realms, so if we can figure out how to put them together that would be a huge step in theoretical physics.”

The researchers plan to expand the dataset as additional observations become available. One important source will be the Dark Energy Bedrock All-Sky Supernova program (DEBASS), which is identifying hundreds of supernovae at distances closer to Earth than those surveyed by DES.

Incorporating these nearby explosions will provide further measurements that scientists can use to investigate the Universe’s expansion and test whether dark energy truly changes over time.

The cosmology findings are available on arXiv here, while the accompanying measurements of host galaxy masses can be found on arXiv here.

The new results build on decades of work by hundreds of astronomers and researchers worldwide. Contributing projects include the Dark Energy Survey, Foundation Supernova Survey, PanStarrs I, Sloan Digital Sky Survey, Supernova Legacy Survey, Carnegie Supernova Project, and the Center for Astrophysics supernova survey.

#565. Cristian Castro Accepts the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award ‘In the Name of Romantic Love’

The pop icon also performed at the Thursday (Oct. 22) ceremony, broadcasted live on Telemundo.

Cristian Castro became emotional on Thursday evening (Oct. 22) as he accepted the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards, delivering a poetic speech inspired by love.

“Romantic love and poetry are the only real things — the truest aspects of our human existence, the firmest thought, the clearest expression that emerges from our spirit and our hearts from the time we are children,” the pop icon remarked upon receiving the award from Mexican actress Jacqueline Bracamontes. “It is like when we first behold the soul — the serene calm of morning dew, the Moon, the majesty of a sunset — and that face, that presence, which fills your entire soul and which you cannot cast out from your being.”

“Throughout my life, romantic love has been my focal point and my true ambition — my firmament and my greatest longing,” continued the singer behind No. 1 hits such as “Amor” and “Azul.” “I accept this award in the name of romantic love and in the name of poetry; they are the most beautiful things I have ever possessed — gifts placed within me by God, alongside my voice.”

Castro, who received the honor in recognition of a glittering career spanning more than three decades and his enduring influence on Latin music, also took to the stage for a special performance during the ceremony, broadcast live on Telemundo and Peacock from the James L. Knight Center in Miami. Together with the Mexican-American duo Ha*Ash, he performed their new collaboration “Antes Que Te Cases” live for the first time.

The Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award honors an artist for an exceptional professional career — someone who has elevated Latin music to a new level on the global stage, remains relevant through their artistic and personal contributions, and whose influence has shaped the development of Latin music worldwide. Previous recipients include Andrea Bocelli, Armando Manzanero, Carlos Santana, José José, Maná, Marco Antonio Solís, Ricardo Arjona and Roberto Carlos, among others.

Castro has solidified his place as one of the defining voices of Latin pop and romantic music. His history on the Billboard charts began in 1992 when “No Podrás” became his first entry on Hot Latin Songs, reaching No. 3. His debut album, Agua Nueva, climbed to No. 2 on Top Latin Pop Albums in January 1993. Since then, he has achieved six No. 1s on Hot Latin Songs, including “Nunca Voy a Olvidarte,” “Amor” and “Azul,” which spent four, eleven and nine weeks at the top, respectively. Years later, Viva El Príncipe, his tribute to legendary Mexican singer José José, spent seven weeks at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums in 2011.

With over 12 million albums sold, Castro continues to connect with audiences through his Nada Solo Éxitos Tour, with performances at major venues such as the Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City and Madison Square Garden in New York.

The 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards brought together the biggest names in Latin music for a night of unforgettable performances, collaborations and special recognitions. In addition to Castro, special honorees this year included Rubén Blades, who received the Billboard Icon Award; Rosalía, who was honored with the Billboard Hall of Fame Award; and Fuerza Regida, who took home the Billboard Vanguard Award.

#566. NYT Pips hints, answers for October 23, 2026

Welcome to your guide to Pips, the latest game in the New York Times catalog.

Released in August 2025, Pips puts a unique spin on dominoes, creating a fun single-player experience that could become your next daily gaming habit.

Currently, if you're stuck, the game only offers to reveal the entire puzzle, forcing you to move on to the next difficulty level and start over. However, we have you covered! Below are piecemeal answers that will serve as hints so that you can find your way through each difficulty level.

If you've ever played dominoes, you'll have a passing familiarity with how Pips is played. As we've shared in our previous hints stories for Pips, the tiles, like dominoes, are placed vertically or horizontally and connect with each other. The main difference between a traditional game of dominoes and Pips is the color-coded conditions you have to address. The touching tiles don't necessarily have to match.

The conditions you have to meet are specific to the color-coded spaces. For example, if it provides a single number, every side of a tile in that space must add up to the number provided. It is possible — and common — for only half a tile to be within a color-coded space.

Here are common examples you'll run into across the difficulty levels:

Number: All the pips in this space must add up to the number.

Equal: Every domino half in this space must be the same number of pips.

Not Equal: Every domino half in this space must have a completely different number of pips.

Less than: Every domino half in this space must add up to less than the number.

Greater than: Every domino half in this space must add up to more than the number.

If an area does not have any color coding, it means there are no conditions on the portions of dominoes within those spaces.

Number (3): Everything in this space must add up to 3. The answer is 1-3, placed horizontally.

Number (3): Everything in this space must add up to 3. The answer is 1-3, placed horizontally; 2-4, placed horizontally.

Equal (4): Everything in this space must be equal to 4. The answer is 2-4, placed horizontally; 4-4, placed vertically.

Equal (5): Everything in this space must be equal to 5. The answer is 5-2, placed vertically; 5-6, placed vertically.

#567. Daily briefing: The tell-tale features of a Denisovan

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Artist depiction of the heavy set facial features of a Denisovan.Credit: Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology/Chinese Academy of Sciences

A low, sloping forehead, a massive brow ridge, rectangle-like eye sockets, flat cheeks, and a moderately elevated bridge of the nose were probably the hallmark features of Denisovans — a mysterious ancient-human species. Using fossilized skull fragments, teeth and jaws, researchers identified some visual features that would have set Denisovans apart from other early-human species, such as the flattened, elongated skull shape. A knowledge of these unique features could help researchers classify other fossils that couldn’t previously be identified as Denisovan.

The emergence of mental-health conditions in teenagers could be forecast by the speed at which certain regions of their brain develop. A study of nearly 12,000 young people in the United States suggests that vulnerability to conditions such as depression in adolescents could involve disruption of the brain’s developmental timeline and could be set in motion by genes that are active before birth. The findings reveal small population-level patterns, says systems neuroscientist Avram Holmes, but can’t be used to track the trajectory of an individual child.

Reference: bioRxiv preprint (not peer reviewed)

A new analysis of ancient artifacts suggests that a woman named Meretneith, who was buried in a lavish tomb around 5,000 years ago, might have been Egypt’s first female ruler. Egyptologists Sue Kelly and Crystal Miller analysed digitally enhanced photographs of serekhs — hieroglyphs that indicate a person ruled at the time of their death — that named the king Djer, and possibly Meretneith, that were found on objects in a separate tomb. They found that one features the goddess Neith, "a symbol no male ruler ever used”, Kelly says, which hints that Meretneith held true royal authority, not that of a consort or regent.

Reference: Prague Egyptological Studies paper

Scientists have mapped the mysterious insula in the human brain in unprecedented detail. The results detail how this region is organized to support the brain’s processing of bodily sensation: one region is responsible for the feeling of pain in some body parts, a second generates sensations such as nausea felt by internal organs and a third ‘talks’ to other brain areas involved in emotion and cognition. The latter area allows for the insula to work with the cortex — the seat of higher-order cognition — to affect how the brain interprets various sensations.

A phase II/III trial of a vaccine against Ebola could see its first doses administered as soon as this week in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where there have been more than 9,500 known cases and more than 4,600 deaths, reports Science. The trial, named Tumaini — Swahili for “hope” — will first use a vaccine called Ervebo that targets a ‘mismatched’ ebolavirus species, ‘Zaire’ — the outbreak in DRC involves the Bundibugyo species. The goal is to add vaccine candidates developed specifically to target Bundibugyo — such as ChAdOx1, developed by a University of Oxford group in the United Kingdom — after they graduate from phase I clinical trials.

Science | 8 min read & Nature | 7 min read (from July)

Robert (Bob) Williamson was a geneticist who dedicated his career to the identification of disease-linked genes and the diagnosis and treatment of single-gene disorders, such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). “He had almost limitless energy and was an inspiring and generous leader,” writes geneticist Kay Davies, who worked alongside Williamson to narrow down the location of the gene responsible for DMD. Williamson then applied this approach to locate the gene that causes CF, and was an early proponent of gene therapy. He has died, aged 88.

“Making climate change visible is only the first step” for a great graphic, argues digital communications researcher Monika Frątczak. Alongside whether a graph or chart is accurate, “we should also ask who is represented, who is missing and whose experience the data allows us to see”, she writes. By tapping into people’s connection to their own land and community, visualizations can inspire deeper engagement — and an emotional response that can lead to real action.

The timings of traffic lights at busy junctions are often decided by algorithms on the basis of the number of vehicles on the road. But who to prioritize isn’t a purely technical decision, and should instead be debated as a matter of public interest, argues computer scientist Xiaowen Tao (陶晓文). (Nature Cities | 5 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03438-9

Today I’ve learned that despite the name, not all white dwarves are white. Physicists found that a handful of these ultra-dense celestial objects can shine in shades of pink, cyan and even green — a colour never spotted before in stars.

#568. Reba McEntire Engaged to Rex Linn: Inside Their Love Story

Reba McEntire found her happy place in fiancé Rex Linn, her partner in life and onscreen. "You better like 'em," she told E! News of the key to their romance. "It's 24/7, so I do like him a lot."

Reba McEntire realized pretty early on that she'd found her, er, happy place in now-fiancé Rex Linn.

It wasn't quite love at first sight, as the country music legend has actually known the actor, 69, since 1991, when they filmed the TV movie The Gambler Returns: The Luck of the Draw.

But when Reba guest starred on his show Young Sheldon in 2020 following the end of her 26-year second marriage to steel guitar player-turned-manager Narvel Blackstock, "It was just like a magnet," she reflected to E! News' Francesca Amiker last year.

Due to COVID-era restrictions, "We didn't get to see each other from January ‘til June 16," the 71-year-old continued, "but we created an intimacy by texting and talking over the telephone that we wouldn't have gotten if we'd have been together all of that time."

Score one for social distancing. Though The Voice coach noted, "We've been pretty much inseparable ever since June 16 of 2020," she's grateful they had the chance to build a love worth writing about from afar.

People tend to "gravitate to the physical so quickly," surmised the music legend, who returns to TV screens alongside Linn with the season three premiere of NBC sitcom Happy's Place. And they were gifted the opportunity to grow as friends first.

"You know the ins and outs of their personality and their faults," the "I'm a Survivor" singer explained. "You love them for the way they are, instead of it being a total attraction and sizing them up because of appearance."

And with Rex, she can't even get the blues.

As she told E!, "He makes me laugh." He also had her reconsidering her future. Twice divorced following splits from steer wrestling champion and rancher Charlie Battles and Narvel (dad to her son Shelby Blackstock, plus Chassidy, Shawna and the late Brandon Blackstock), he had her believing the third time would be the charm.

"I'm truly committed to Rex," she explained to E!. "So if that's something he feels totally strong about, that's fine with me. He's never been married before. So if he wants to experience that, I'm OK with that."

Really OK with it considering the sparkly new left-hand accessory she was flashing at the Emmys 2025.

And after Live From E!: 2025 Emmys correspondent Zuri Hall referred to Rex as her fiancé, Reba revealed they'd already settled into their happy wife, happy life era, regardless of marital status.

"We're having a blast on Happy's Place," she shared, "and so glad to be here tonight."

While they've re-upped their love story indefinitely, their packed schedules have created a bit of a cliffhanger situation.

"We'e just waiting until we have an open spot to have the wedding," Reba explained to E News at the NBC Backlot Pass event in August. "Get it planned. Print those invitations."

And while the details are still in flux, friends and family shouldn't expect a stuff black tie affair.

"It'll be a lot of fun," she vowed to E! News last November. "It's gonna be a nontraditional wedding because that’s Rex and me. We like comfort, we love friends, we love food."

Indeed, their yearly Valentine's Day tradition sees them hit up a nearby Sonic (perhaps the inspiration for their nicknames Sugar Tot and Tater Tot) while Christmas means popcorn and candy.

"We have our Christmas on Christmas Eve and he likes to go see movies," Reba explained to E! News in December 2024, "so we'll do that first thing in the morning before the crowds hit the theaters, Then we'll come back and we'll have our meals."

Joked Reba, "You noticed I said 'meals,' because we'll have lunch and supper and probably a midnight snack. That will be our tradition."

After all, breaking bread is part of what pulled them together back in 2020.

"Rex texted me and said, 'You're coming to LA? Let's have dinner,'" Reba recalled to Today in 2023. While she didn't know why he requested the date, she continued, "I wanted to get in to see Rex so bad I could hardly stand it. We were inseparable."

Little has changed with the two continuing to mix business and pleasure.

"Rex and I met on The Gambler movie in '91, so we're used to working together and also being together as partners and buddies and lovers," Reba explained to E!. "It just works out."

Of course, she added, "You better like 'em—all the time. It's 24/7, so I do like him a lot."

As the musician prepares to re-enter her bridal era, look back on all the high notes the she's hit over the years.

(Originally published Sept. 15, 2025, at 7:19 a.m. PT)

Reba McEntire first met her special somebody Rex Linn on the set of Kenny Rogers' 1991 movie The Gambler Returns: The Luck of the Draw, in which she played lead Burgundy Jones and he made a cameo."He gets a big kick out of it," the country music star recalled on Today in April 2023. "He says his part was riding into a saloon on a 4-year-old colt and going, 'Yeehaw!' and riding out."Over the years, the two stayed in contact as friends. However, Reba was already married to Narvel Blackstock—becoming stepmom to his kids Shawna, Chassidy and Brandon Blackstock after tying the knot in 1989 and welcoming son Shelby Blackstock the following year—and it would be decades before she and Rex struck up a romance.

Four years after Reba and Narvel divorced near the end of 2015, she crossed paths with Rex again. This time, it was on Young Sheldon, where she made a guest appearance and he had a recurring role."Rex texted me and said, 'You going to be in town?'" Reba recalled on The Jennifer Hudson Show in July 2025. "I said, 'Yeah.' He said, 'Well, let's go to dinner.'"After enjoying a meal with friends, the actress continued, they headed to a wine bar, where Reba ordered some tater tots and Rex determined, "That's your nickname from here on out."Luckily for fans of the Tots (she's "Tater Tot" and he's "Sugar Tot"), there's a photo from that special night."Had a fantastic dinner with this Oklahoma girl," Rex wrote on Instagram in January 2020. "Tater Tots and Ketchup included."

With their romance beginning at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, Reba and Rex were forced to date long-distance. However, this enabled them to connect on a deeper level."Because of the pandemic, we didn't get to see each other from January to June 16, but we created an intimacy by texting and talking over the telephone that we wouldn't have gotten if we had been together all that time," the singer explained to E! News in April 2024. "So it was very special, and it was a great way of finding out about each other without ever touching. We've been pretty much inseparable since June 16 of 2020. It was a wonderful way to get to know each other better."

Reba and Rex went public with their relationship that fall."It's good to have a person to talk to, laugh with, get into subjects about what's going on, discussions about our past, our family, funny stories, him being an actor, me being an actress," the Grammy winner said while confirming their romance on an October 2020 episode of her podcast Living & Learning. "He's very into my music. I'm very into his career. It's just great getting to talk to somebody who I find very interesting, very funny, very smart and is interested in me, too."That same month, Reba and Rex gave fans glimpses into their life together, posting photos of them from their time in Montana.

Soon afterwards, the "I'm a Survivor" artist and the CSI: Miami actor made their red carpet debut as a couple at the 2020 CMA Awards, which she hosted.

Fans got more insight into Reba and Rex's romance when he was a guest on her podcast the following year.During their discussion, they looked back at how they've leaned on each other during tough times, which include the March 2020 death of Reba's mother Jacqueline McEntire after her battle with cancer."It was later on that I was texting you, and I told you about mamma—that we just found out that she had bladder cancer," the musician said on the October 2021 episode of Living & Learning. "And you said, 'Hey, you just feel free to call me anytime you need to talk.' And I just quit texting and then we've been talking ever since."Rex also remembered how Reba called him and offered her condolences after his mother died in 1998."We talked for about 25 minutes, and I never forgot it," he added. "It was amazing, it was uplifting, it was really special and little did I know 20 years later, 21 years later I'd be doing the same thing with her on the phone."

The couple had a fancy night out at the 2022 Oscars, where Reba performed "Somehow You Do."

In August 2022, it was announced that Reba and Rex were taking their love to the small screen by playing married couple Sunny and Buck Barnes on Big Sky.

"We love working together because when we're at home, we get to practice, rehearse and he's a rehearsal schedule freak," Reba told ABC Audio in 2022. "He makes sure I know my lines before I ever go on stage."

The pair continued on their journey as both costars in life and work by acting in The Hammer.

And their castmates agreed they seemed pretty happy working on Happy's Place, which premiered in 2024.

"It's adorable and oftentimes ... we're taking a five-minute break or we're having breakfast or lunch and you look over and we have a bar set—it takes place at Happy's Place—and you look over and they're in a booth at the bar," Melissa Peterman, who also starred on Reba, told People in October 2024. "And it looks like they're legitimately on a date at a restaurant just sitting together being so adorably cute."

In fact, Reba noted she could see them being happy long term as husband and wife."Totally, if that's what Rex wants," the "What If" artist, who was married to Charlie Battles before her union with Narvel, told E! in April 2024. "I've been married twice. After the second one dissolved, I don't have much faith in being bound by a piece of paper or a ring. But I'm truly committed to Rex. So if that's something he feels totally strong about, that's fine with me. He's never been married before. So if he wants to experience that, I'm OK with that."

Five years after their first dinner, Reba and Rex recreated the photo from that date.

What do you say to a proposal? Well, Reba said yes to Rex, with them confirming their engagement to E! News at the 2025 Emmys.E! News learned that the couple had gotten engaged "a few months ago" and that "they are very happy."

#570. Pride, prestige, profile - the great Ballon d'Or campaign

Ousmane Dembele won the Ballon d"Or in 2025 and is one of 10 PSG players listed for it this year

An emotional Ousmane Dembele had barely settled back into his chair at Paris' historic Theatre du Chatelet last September, gold-dipped orb in hand, when campaigns for this year's men's Ballon d'Or prize began to whirr into action.

Entourages roused their candidates, media revelled in the hype. Who deserved the award in 2026? A World Cup year, no less, in which the narrative occasionally became not just which players could lead their country to glory, but how doing so would help them secure football's biggest individual accolade.

"The Ballon d'Or has been discussed every single day," said European football expert Guillem Balague on BBC Sport's Euro Leagues podcast.

"Quite clearly it follows the pattern of society, where it puts a lot of emphasis on the individual - it's harder to understand why a collective works, it becomes very easy to understand why one dribbles or doesn't dribble."

Clamour for the spotlight only increased as the red-carpet ceremony neared.

"You can't underestimate the PR machine that some clubs and some players are going to use," added French football journalist Julien Laurens.

Managers and sporting directors talked up their charges, and questioned why others on their squad did not make the 30-man shortlist.

Deco branded it a "huge scandal" that Barcelona pair Raphinha and Pedri missed out, but backed Lamine Yamal as overwhelming favourite to win it. Not, he says, because he is also a Barca player, but "because I like football".

Star names have appeared frequently in the media. Lamine Yamal himself insisted he will not "beg for anything" - after last year saying he dreamed of "winning many" - but suggested the prize should not merely go to the top goalscorer.

Paris St-Germain manager Luis Enrique confessed he is "bored of the Ballon dâOr" - although with a record 10 PSG players on the shortlist, perhaps he wishes to keep out of the debate. Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia talked each other up to BBC Sport.

"We can cut it in two," joked Dembele. "Honestly, he deserves it, the season he had was exceptional." Kvaratskhelia responded: "Of course it's him!"

A 'Kvara d'Or' campaign in Georgia celebrated the country's favourite fleet-footed son.

"I think for the big nations it's really difficult to understand what [winning] would mean for the small country," the winger explained.

Kylian Mbappe, who Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho compared to the original Ronaldo, was less subtle than most in his pitch to win the award for the first time.

"I always think I'm the best but everyone has their own opinion," professed the Frenchman, now the all-time World Cup top goalscorer. "Of course, this year could be good for me to win the Ballon d'Or - but journalists vote."

Indeed - since a short spell of national team captains and managers also voting ended in 2015 - the 30-player shortlist drawn up by the publications France Football and L'Equipe has been voted on by one journalist from each of the top 100 Fifa-ranked nations.

The deadline has passed. The winner has already been chosen.

What does it mean to win the Ballon d'Or?

James Kirkham, a sports brand strategist who has worked with top clubs and players, including Harry Kane, says the build-up has had an election feel.

"You're going out, canvassing, getting your vote and making sure you shore up certain blocks from certain countries, and why wouldn't you?" adds Kirkham.

The lobbying is not for everyone. Max Eberl, Bayern Munich's board member for sport, championed Kane and Michael Olise but said the best players, external "are the ones who don't need to run a campaign".

Mbappe's compatriot, Jean-Pierre Papin, winner of the award in 1991, meanwhile told French TV:, external "I like Kylian a lot, he's a record-breaker. However, there comes a point when it's all about me, me, me and me."

Mbappe did make an interesting observation, alluding to the dominance of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo - the pair won a combined 13 in a 15-year period between 2008 and 2023.

"My idea of the Ballon d'Or comes from the Messi and Ronaldo era - you don't give it to ordinary players, you give it âto players who are different," explained Mbappe.

AC Milan's Kaka was the last recipient before Messi and Ronaldo's tug-of-war began, the Brazilian pipping the young pair to the prize in 2007.

That was a year after fledgling social media platforms Facebook and Twitter launched to the public. Nokia dominated mobile phone markets, people took digital cameras on nights out.

The world had changed immeasurably by the time Messi won for an eighth time in 2023.

"Today everything moves at the speed of light," explains former AC Milan chief executive and sporting director Ariedo Braida, who witnessed the club land seven awards, from Ruud Gullit to Marco van Basten's treble, George Weah, Andriy Shevchenko and Kaka.

"Fans follow individuals - the players - rather than the club themselves. It's a widespread phenomenon, which we see, for example, in politics too.

"Once upon a time, you'd be a Milan fan and go to watch Milan. Today, everything is live and with the Champions League you always get to see all the great stars straight away.

"I must say this makes me feel a bit nostalgic, because the event is always immediate. Anticipation creates that sense of longing which has now disappeared."

Are fans now more invested in star names than clubs?

Messi and Ronaldo's brilliance, and often tribal online following, has also driven an increased emphasis on individual records - among fans, media and the players who grew up dreaming of emulating them.

"You could argue we are in a more interesting time because for basically 15 years it was Messi v Ronaldo and it certainly feels more open. It is a different play now," adds Kirkham.

"The social noise is deafening, relentless, all-consuming - every fan has an insatiable appetite, every point is riffed on, reacted to, but you also have this domino effect in microcosms of the media on every platform."

Clips go viral - a great goal, magical piece of skill, a dazzling dribble - but so do opinions.

"Now a solitary word on a broadcast can get played out as tweets, reacted to by creators and ex-players in video content that exists on reels and shorts and stories, that gets back-played through radio and on TV screens," adds Kirkham.

"It's the whole ecosystem, the manner in which it amplifies across these different spaces and platforms, then it generates narratives.

"No-one is doing anything wrong, creating something they believe is resonating with their audience. But en masse that is a machine, a fierce output that is generated for a player or against a player or whatever that may be."

Braida, who was at Barcelona when Messi won the 2015 prize, would agree: "These days, media exposure is absolutely crucial. With the advent of social media, the world has changed radically compared to my day.

"There's been a global transformation, and today we live in a small global village, because with the internet you can reach everywhere in real time."

Harry Kane reflects on potential Ballon d'Or success

Michael Owen tells a story about how when Liverpool boss Gerard Houllier rang to break the news he had won the award in 2001, the 22-year-old did not even know what the Ballon d'Or was.

Owen engaged in a photoshoot at Liverpool's Melwood training ground a fortnight before the images were distributed to the media, with the striker officially presented the trophy on the Anfield pitch before a game against Derby County.

He was the first winner playing for an English club since Manchester United's George Best in 1968, the period in between dominated by Italian, Spanish and German teams.

From its launch in 1956 until 1995, when Weah became the first and so-far only African player to win it, only European players were eligible.

Only in 2007 did the award became truly global, open to players from any club - not just those representing European teams. Not until 2011 was it awarded at a glamorous ceremony. And only in 2018 was the women's prize launched.

"Winning the Ballon d'Or has an extremely positive impact," adds Braida. "We at AC Milan bought Kaka for around 7.5m euros and sold him for 67m euros [to Real Madrid].

"I must tell you, however, that in 2008, following his Ballon d'Or win in 2007, Manchester City made us a written offer of 105m euros. We're talking about a written offer, not a sounding-out or mere words.

"We were probably still in the early stages of certain commercial developments at that time, but now it clearly has a massive impact. Even back then, his value increased fivefold and winning the Ballon d'Or brought him global exposure and fame."

For someone like Three Lions captain Kane, hoping to become the first English winner in 25 years and only the fifth of all time, the prestige is huge - especially with the ceremony held in London to mark the 70th anniversary of Stanley Matthews winning the inaugural prize.

"It would be a massive achievement if it did happen," Kane said on Wednesday, having remained coy on his own chances.

Kane has done his share of recent interviews but others, such as Rio Ferdinand on Bayern's official social accounts, have made his case for him. "Ballon d'Or!"

He is, after all, vying to become Bayern's first winner since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge's second successive triumph in 1981. Not since Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer 30 years ago has it returned to the Bundesliga.

Bayern will also remember the case of Robert Lewandowski, who was widely tipped as favourite in 2020, scoring at an astonishing rate as the Bavarians won all six trophies available, including the Champions League, before the ceremony was cancelled because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The Poland striker, who finished runner-up to Messi the following season, told BBC Sport last year the prize has become "part football, partly politics" and was "more commercial" than its counterpart, The Best Fifa Men's Player award.

Ballon d'Or snubs can cut deep. Franck Ribery said it felt "like a robbery" when he missed out to Ronaldo in 2013. Real Madrid boycotted the 2024 ceremony when they learned Manchester City midfielder Rodri would scoop the gong instead of Vinicius Junior.

"In Brazil, the hype is also giant," explains Caique Andrade, international football reporter at Globo. "When Vini didn't win the 2024 Ballon d'Or, there was a lot of commotion about it."

It may be an individual award, but winning is huge for clubs, too.

"This means an incredible impact in terms of popularity, visibility and also financial returns for the club," explains Braida. "Today, with the rise of social media and followers - factors that shape commercial aspects - this is even more true."

Kirkham concludes: "It is a global point - that means more audience and more eyeballs, and that means more money around the world."

#572. Roku Pro Series OLED TV Review (2026)

If you have OLED TV aspirations but an in-this-economy bank balance, good news: Roku just entered the chat with its first-ever OLED, and it starts at a reasonable $1,000—not counting inevitable future discounts, like the recent October Prime Day deal that lopped off $300. Of course, price rarely tells the full television story, like whether a budget OLED can stand up to, say, a high-end QLED or midrange mini-LED.

Here’s the story: The Roku Pro Series OLED is a very good TV, better than its price tag would suggest, though not without a few compromises. Colors dazzle, black levels go deep, and Roku’s software continues to yield the best user experience. It’s not blazingly bright, and your size options are few (55 or 65 inches), but on the whole this should please anyone making a move from an older, lesser screen.

Although Roku provides only a small printed quick-start guide, there’s nothing complicated about setting up this TV. The two tool-free feet attach with large thumbscrews and can be set at two different heights—great if you want to, say, raise the screen a bit higher so your soundbar doesn’t block it.

From there, Roku’s friendly UI walks you through the usual configuration steps, many of which you can complete on your phone (as opposed to navigating onscreen menus with the remote, always a slower process).

Four well-marked HDMI ports reside on the left side of the Roku Pro Series, set close enough to the edge that they’re easy to reach. The top one, clearly labeled “eARC,” is painted with Roku’s trademark purple for quick at-a-glance identification, while the bottom two—120-Hz ports intended for gaming—are white. (Why two? It’s a bit unusual, yes, but splendid for those who operate more than one console.) The TV also supplies the usual coaxial input for a traditional cable or antenna hookup, an optical audio input for older soundbars and an Ethernet port if you want to bypass Wi-Fi.

Speaking of which, it’s a bit disappointing that Roku opted for Wi-Fi 5 here instead of Wi-Fi 6 or later. That said, my Eero Pro router also tops out at Wi-Fi 5, and it’s likely the same situation in plenty of other households. I encountered zero issues in terms of connection reliability, stability, or performance.

The Roku operating system continues to offer the most intuitive and novice-friendly TV viewing experience, marked by its colorful, oversize app icons and simple menus. There’s a bit more UI customization available now than in Rokus past, like the option to display icons in four columns instead of three. And there’s a sense of whimsy here not found elsewhere, including the lively “Roku City” screensaver that appears when the TV is idle. You can also opt for Roku Backdrops, an art-themed screensaver that does a solid Samsung The Frame impression.

Ads do crop up in various places—nearly a third of the home screen, a banner at the bottom of the menu screen, etc.—but they’re mostly streaming-related, not obnoxiously product-oriented like in Amazon’s and Google’s UIs.

One small gripe: There are still some streaming apps—HBO Max, Paramount+, etc.—that don’t let you sign into your account via app or QR code, even though their Google TV counterparts do. So be prepared for the occasional hassle of having to manually navigate onscreen keyboards with the remote.

Thankfully, Roku’s remote still rocks, with a cheerful purple navigation pad, dedicated play/pause and shuttle buttons, a programmable shortcut button, and side-mounted volume and mute controls. It’s more comfortable and intuitive than most remotes and is backlit. Unfortunately, it’s not rechargeable, an annoying oversight for a “Pro Series” TV. And its push-to-talk voice controls are fine for the likes of basic searches and playback functions but are constrained to Roku’s UI; you don’t get the added “smarts” afforded by Alexa+ and Google Assistant. (The exception: Roku’s branded smart-home gear, such as security cameras and light bulbs, can be controlled via voice commands.)

At least if the remote goes missing in the couch cushions (or an entirely different room, which is where I tried it), a handy remote-finder button on the right side of the TV will trigger “Here I am!” beeps.

To test the Roku Pro Series, I watched a wide range of sports, movies, and TV shows and fired up my Xbox Series X. As with other budget OLEDs, the colors impress; the brightness, not so much.

I started by streaming Solo: A Star Wars Story on Disney+. The first five minutes take place in the dark (literally and figuratively) underbelly of Corellia, and I’ve found that many TVs struggle here with contrast and brightness; several of these early scenes can look muddy or just plain dim. Roku’s OLED fared well on the contrast front, but I found myself wishing for a bit more visibility when Han lays out his plan to Kira and, later, confronts Lady Proxima. Even watching in a relatively dark room, those moments revealed suboptimal brightness.

Next up, the white-hallway scene in Mythic Quest, season 3, episode 1—a great measure of both contrast and black levels. Ian Grimm’s shirt appeared dark as night and juxtaposed perfectly against the smooth white walls. And within those walls, different shades appeared in different areas as the characters walked around; the TV expertly contrasted all of them. Did I find myself wishing for slightly whiter whites? Yes. Did I enjoy the scene any less? No.

While I had the Apple TV app running, I tuned into some live MLB soccer. The action: sharp and smooth (and dull, obviously, because soccer), and the same was true when I switched over to an NFL game on DirecTV. That’s as expected with a 120-Hz refresh rate.

Speaking of which, that rate, coupled with low-latency game mode (which kicked on automatically) served my Xbox experiences well. From the 1930s palette of the cartoonish Cuphead to the candy-colored arcade racing of Burnout: Paradise, everything looked crisp and vivid, with fast response times and zero blur.

For my color investigations, I clicked into Planet Earth II on HBO Max, Pixar’s Coco on Disney+, various “8K” nature videos on YouTube, and an Inglorious Basterds 4K Blu-ray played on the Xbox. Across the board, the Roku Pro Series produced vibrant, richly detailed color—but with less of the “pop” I’ve witnessed on high-end LG and Sony OLEDs. That’s partially due to the panel’s limited brightness.

Whether that’s a bad thing is open for debate; some would argue that higher-end OLEDs oversaturate, the shiny colors more of a distraction than an enhancement. Discuss.

A notable Roku innovation is Smart Picture Max, which automatically detects the type of content you’re watching and adjusts various display settings accordingly. Though it’s hard to gauge the impact of this on things like color and brightness, there’s one clearly quantifiable benefit: motion-smoothing. Smart Picture Max disables it for most TV shows and movies, meaning you don’t get the dreaded soap-opera effect. That alone gives the Pro Series a leg up over most OLEDs, which require manual tinkering to disable this heinous feature (and again to re-enable it for sports and gaming, the only situations in which it’s not heinous).

The one catch here is that any Dolby Vision content overrides Smart Picture Max, leaving motion-smoothing switched on. Fortunately, Roku makes it refreshingly easy to modify that and other picture settings; just press the star button on the remote. I found (and toggled off) smoothing with just a few clicks. Another nice perk: Any change you make applies instantly to whatever you’re viewing, so you can immediately gauge whether it’s what you want; you don’t have to exit the menu to see the results.

On the audio front, the presence of Dolby Atmos does nothing to improve the TV’s speakers, which produce plenty of volume but get harsh and shrill the higher you go. Indeed, the opening measures of Nick Perito’s “The Green Leaves of Summer” in Inglorious Basterds were deeply unpleasant, even at a modest volume. This came as something of a surprise, as Roku’s previous Pro Series TV sounded much better overall. The speakers here are tolerable at low volumes in a small room; for everything else, you’re going to want a soundbar.

In the end, Roku’s first OLED won’t win over any die-hard fans of premium panels; it’s a budget model through and through, probably on par with LG’s similarly affordable B6. But it’s still an OLED, with all the vivid color, pitch-black black, and strong contrast that technology affords. And the Roku remote, interface, and automated image adjustments contribute to a splendid user experience. Watch for the next sale (Black Friday, anyone?) and you’ll feel like you’re getting a steal.

#573. The EU wants an AI revolution. But on whose terms?

As the US and China race ahead, the European Union seeks to boost its economy with AI. Can it compete while protecting workers, safety and the climate?

Step-dancers spun across the circular stage in the middle of a dark hall, entrancing an audience of policymakers and tech bosses. Not simply another bureaucratic conference, the International AI Summit, hosted in Dublin this week, aspired to something more spectacular — a grand announcement that Europe is ready for its artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.

Among the more than 1,500 expected guests were Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis and Microsoft president Brad Smith, in addition to high-ranking European Union and Irish officials. The event was a key part of Ireland's term as president of the EU Council, but a lack of critical voices to counterbalance the AI enthusiasm on display has drawn accusations of tech boosterism.

The summit was "almost like a party political broadcast on behalf of AI," Barry O'Sullivan, an AI professor at University College Cork, told DW.

The overarching theme was how to use AI to get Europe's sluggish economy moving, boost innovation and catch up with the US and China.

On panels packed with senior executives, the potential benefits were made clear: detecting early signs of cancer, improving warnings of extreme weather, and optimising power distribution to save energy. Turning those promises into reliable services, however, still requires testing and validation.

Ireland's interest in these issues doesn't come purely from goodwill towards its fellow EU member states. The country hosts the European operations of several of the world's largest technology companies, and relies heavily on the taxation of multinational firms. Foreign-owned multinationals paid €28.8 billion in corporation tax in 2025, accounting for 87% of the total, excluding exceptional Apple tax proceeds. That includes pharmaceuticals and other sectors, not just technology.

This means Dublin has a clear interest in shaping European rules while keeping investors on board. But Europe's financial firepower remains far behind America's: Private AI investment reached $286 billion (about €253 billion) in the US in 2025, compared with $21 billion (€18.6 billion) in Europe, according to Stanford University's AI Index.

But does Europe even need to compete on the same terms? O'Sullivan thinks it should focus on its own strengths, including industrial robotics and specialised applications: "We have a unique kind of AI opportunity in Europe, and that's what we should back."

Using foreign models could help European businesses move faster. But it also leaves them dependent on suppliers elsewhere, which can change prices, restrict access and decide which capabilities to release.

EU representatives at the summit were quick to underline that rules were now in place to reap AI's benefits while mitigating its risks.

Michael McGrath, the Irish commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection, spoke of a balance between AI's potential and the "appropriate guardrails" required to ensure trust.

The AI Act bans certain practices and imposes stronger requirements on sensitive uses. Its Omnibus amendments, in force since July 2026, aim to simplify compliance, though have als delyed some safeguards. Rules covering areas including employment and education now apply from December 2027; those for AI embedded in regulated products from August 2028.

The Commission has said that companies need time to adjust to new standards and guidance. Critics, however, believe protections being delayed under pressure to compete.

For O'Sullivan, regulation and innovation are not contradictory. "The idea that you can't have regulation and innovation is just a nonsense," he said, pointing to pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

For protesters outside, assurances made by politicians and tech firms ring hollow. Paul Murphy, an Irish lawmaker from the socialist People Before Profit party, argued that even though Europe's regulations are strong than those in the US, the bar remains low. With the latest amendments, he sees a move towards deregulation.

"Big tech is setting the pace and everybody's expected to just get on board," he told DW.

Instead, he wants civil society, trade unions and politicians to discuss how the technology should develop and how limited resources like water and electricity should be used.

Inside, union representative Fionnuala Ní Bhrógáin, one of the few critical voices on stage, questioned who would benefit from higher productivity. Optimization, she said, can put higher pressure on workers.

Murphy, too, fears an increased pressure to work faster, with less autonomy and more supervision. Whether an hour saved on emails becomes time to think, or leads to more assignments, depends on employers' decisions and workers' bargaining power.

O'Sullivan, on the other hand, said that AI removing mundane tasks gives employees "more time to think, and to be more creative in their jobs."

In Ireland, the question of resources is particularly pressing. Data centres used 23% of the country's metered electricity in 2025. That includes cloud storage and other services, not just AI. Murphy argued that their expansion raises household bills and undermines climate goals.

Renewable energy could help meet demand. But additional clean electricity must also replace fossil fuels, while housing and other industries need grid capacity too.

"The sustainability of AI is a huge problem," O'Sullivan agreed, calling for the sector to reduce its overall energy footprint.

Back inside the hall, even industry leaders acknowledged the need for boundaries. Hassabis, the chief scientist of Alphabet, called recent AI hacking incidents "early warning shots" and advocated international oversight. Microsoft president Smith said: "We need law. We need regulation."

Their warnings follow concrete failures. During cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI models bypassed isolation controls, hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, Hugging Face, which hosts AI models and datasets. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, the results could have been much worse. Anthropic separately disclosed unintended actions by its AI on real websites, including a ​false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.

Speakers on and off the stage agreed: The incidents show just how difficult it can be to keep increasingly autonomous systems under control. Developers' assurances alone cannot guarantee safety. Nor can regulation eliminate every risk. But for O'Sullivan and Murphy, it remains essential.

Europe wants to shape AI without compromising on the benefits its promises.This balancing act is a difficult one, involving choices about investment, resources and the distribution of gains. Even a spectacular opening performance cannot dance around those questions.

#574. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

The "eclipse of the century" will plunge some of ancient Egypt's most spectacular sites into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027. These temples, tombs and monuments are inside the path of totality.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027, has an ancient feel. It will certainly be a celestial event for the ages — at 6 minutes 23 seconds, it will feature the longest totality on land of the 21st century and the longest anywhere until 2114. However, its point of greatest eclipse occurs just a few miles from Thebes, the magnificent religious and political capital of ancient Egypt's Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom.

On the east bank of the mighty Nile is Luxor, the great city of the living, with its massive temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor. On its west bank is the city of the dead, which includes the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Hatshepsut. Modern Luxor, population 285,000, is set to become a focal point for eclipse chasers on Aug. 2, 2027, and will attract many thousands of international visitors. They'll come for the forecasted 0% chance of clouds and the era-defining duration of totality, but also to tour ancient Egypt's temples and monuments.

The chances of actually witnessing totality at any of the major temples are probably slim. Still, almost every eclipse chaser headed to Luxor will want to tour them before or after the eclipse. Visitors should be prepared for extreme August heat and check official opening and access arrangements before planning to watch the eclipse at any archaeological site. Certified eclipse glasses are essential during the partial phases; only during totality, when the sun is completely covered, is it safe to look without them.

Not all of ancient Egypt will experience totality. Egypt's top-ranking monument, the Pyramids at Giza, near Cairo, lies north of the path of totality and will get a 95% partial solar eclipse. Abu Simbel, on the shores of Lake Nasser south of Aswan, will also see a 92% partial solar eclipse. No matter, Luxor is home to some of the world's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments. Here are its temples, necropolises and palaces — and those nearby, also in the 160-mile (257-kilometer)-wide path of totality — that will have the moon's umbral shadow fall upon them on Aug. 2, 2027. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Start of totality and duration: 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

Dedicated to the god Amun-Ra — a fusion of the hidden god of the sun Amun and the ancient sun god Ra — this vast temple complex will be the hottest ticket in town for the eclipse. One of Egypt's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments, it's a place designed by ancient astronomers — the winter solstice sunrise still illuminates the innermost sanctuary. Access arrangements for eclipse day have yet to be confirmed, so keep an eye on official announcements before making plans to watch totality from the complex.

Start of totality and duration: 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

This is one of Egypt's best-preserved ancient temples and a must-see during the 2027 eclipse. It's on the banks of the Nile near the city center, so it's relatively easy to visit. Dedicated to the god Amun, it is known for its beautiful pillars and intricate carvings. A 75-foot (23 meters) tall obelisk on the east side of its entrance will point at the eclipsed sun almost directly overhead on Aug. 2, 2027. Its missing right-hand obelisk is in the Place de la Concorde, Paris.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

This incredible necropolis is home to the tombs of the pharaohs and is a testament to the advanced engineering and architectural skills of the ancient Egyptians. Of course, you don't want to be underground for totality, but some of the tombs are a must-see. Your tickets include entry to any three tombs of your choice from those open that day, with extra tickets available for the really impressive ones—the spectacular KV17 (Seti I), small but iconic KV62 (Tutankhamun), and KV9 (Ramesses V & VI). The latter's Corridor G has a ceiling decoration that may depict a deep partial solar eclipse from 1143 BC.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

If one temple is best suited to crowds for an eclipse, it's this vast, open-air gem dedicated to the legendary queen who became pharaoh. However, with almost no shade, it could be the least practical option. Three huge terraces rise above the desert floor and into the cliffs of Deir el-Bahari to the west. It's an absolute masterpiece.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

This is where we get to temples that are fairly well known, but likely won't have as much pressure on them from eclipse chasers as the big three — Karnak, Luxor and Hatshepsut. However, anyone looking for ways to get temple architecture into images of an eclipse at zenith should look no further than these two large stone statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III. Behind them are the ruins of the largest temple in the Theban Necropolis.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

Getting off the beaten track in August 2027 will be near-impossible, but here's an option — the Mortuary Temple of Ramesses III. Featuring towering stone columns, colorful reliefs (despite being 3,200 years old) and famous carvings, it's bypassed by tour buses heading straight for Hatshepsut.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

Another temple that, without Karnak and Luxor nearby, would be rammed with visitors, is the Ramesseum — the mortuary temple of Ramesses II. Featuring the remains of a huge fallen statue that inspired Shelley's poem Ozymandias, it's in an area once used by the artisans who built the royal tombs, and slightly off the tourist route.

Start of totality and duration: 1:02 p.m. EEST; 5 minutes, 47 seconds

If you want to avoid the scrum of eclipse chasers in Luxor on and around Aug. 2, the Temple of Khnum could be an option. Located in Esna, about 34 miles (55 kilometers) south of Luxor, the so-called 'Rainbow Temple' (for its colorful ceilings) is dedicated to the ram-headed creator god Khnum. Dating from the Greco-Roman era, there's a vast Hypostyle Hall that sits below modern street level, which could be good for some shade.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 15 seconds

If you want to escape Luxor but (almost) keep its long totality, head to Qena, 40 miles (65 km) north, where one of Egypt's best-preserved and most beautiful temples stands. Dendera was the cult center for Hathor, one of the most important and popular deities in ancient Egypt and known as the 'lady of the sky.' The temple's entrance has six massive columns, each decorated with Hathor's head, and its ceiling features astronomical engravings.

Start of totality and duration: 1:04 p.m. EEST; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Another great option for those who prioritize ancient Egyptian surroundings over the longest possible totality is the Temple of Horus, one of the most striking and best-preserved temples in ancient Egypt. About 68 miles (110 km) south of Luxor, it's dedicated to the sun and sky god Horus, one of the main gods in ancient Egypt, whose right eye represents the sun and left eye the moon. The temple's stone roofs are intact, so its Hypostyle Halls, inner chambers and central sanctuary provide some shade.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.
