#576. Inside Alexander Skarsgård's & Tuva Novotny's Private Family World

Alexander Skarsgård is pretty out there with his work and red carpet looks, but the Wicker star is extremely private when it comes to his home life with actress Tuva Novotny and their son.

Alexander Skarsgård isn't a wicker man in real life, but he's made of all the right stuff as far as Tuva Novotny is concerned.

And at least one key component of the Swedish actors' romance is that they're on the same page about keeping their careers separate from their personal business.

"For many years, I wouldn’t do interviews, I wouldn’t watch my own stuff," Novotny, who shares a 4-year-old son with the Wicker star and has two daughters from a previous relationship, told Vogue Scandinavia in 2024. "I don’t see myself as a public person. My job is public and then what I do outside of work is super private."

And that's obviously Å-OK with Skarsgård. Back when he was single and living out of a suitcase, he told The Guardian in 2018, he didn't talk about relationships as "a way to protect it."

“When I was a kid, that’s how my father dealt with it," he explained. "I wouldn’t say it kept him sane, because he’s pretty crazy, but somewhat. The fact that he protected his private life so much, and protected my mum who is not an actor or a public figure.”

Skarsgård is the eldest of actor Stellan Skarsgård and physician My Skarsgård's six children, plus he has two half-brothers from his dad's second marriage.

"Eventually when it’s time to have kids and stuff, I want to have nine," the Big Little Lies alum quipped. "I want to beat my dad.”

Skarsgård's own branch of the sprawling tree sprouted toward the end of 2022, but he didn't confirm that he had become a dad until March 2023, when he accepted the congratulations of a reporter—and a stuffed animal from a well-wisher—on the Succession fourth season premiere red carpet.

They've never shared how they met, but he and Novotny have now been together for seven years and they make their home in the Södermalm district of Stockholm, where they're surrounded by members of Skarsgård's "very big, very tight family."

"Lots of drinking, lots of smoking, lots of crazy, eccentric people," he told The Times in an interview published Oct. 17. "But a very fun environment to grow up in. To this day my entire extended family live within a 10-minute walk from here."

As for his own household, the 50-year-old quipped that his partner's teenage daughters think he's "deeply uncool, of course." But since becoming a dad, his "priorities have changed."

Skarsgård explained, "It was easy, before, to be spontaneous. I'm quite adventurous, so if an opportunity arose to go to the South Pole or Greenland, or sail across the Atlantic, I did it."

He now saves most of his risk-taking for the screen, as his role in Wicker—about a lonely fisherwoman who has the town weaver craft a perfect husband out of the titular material and he proceeds to fulfill her every need—would attest.

Skarsgård is still interested in exploring the world, he noted, "but spending time with my boy is incredibly precious. It's made me more discerning. I don't feel the need to work nonstop the way I did before. If I take on a job it has got to be special enough to warrant being away."

When his father starred in 2025's Sentimental Value as a self-absorbed filmmaker who's estranged from his adult daughters, Stellan and his kids had a good time poking fun at the assumptions that the role was at least somewhat true to life.

Skarsgård told The Times that, while he didn't talk to his dad much about work when he was younger, preferring to make his "own mistakes and stupid decisions," the 75-year-old now "feels like a friend who's also a colleague that you're shooting the s--t with."

But when he was a kid the True Blood alum did wish for a more average upbringing.

"My dream was for my family to be normal and fit in and be like everybody else’s family," Skarsgård said during a sit-down with Stellan for Variety last December. "For you to have a briefcase, that would’ve been fantastic, rather than a weird tote bag that you found in India."

Now it's Skarsgård's son who will one day have thoughts about his father's beguiling see-through Saint Laurent footwear, but it's the chaotic portion of his childhood the Emmy winner wants to avoid passing on, not the creative part.

On her end, Novotny "wasn't really interested in performing at all" when she was a child, she told Vogue, but growing up in her own big, artistic family with her actress mom, director dad and five siblings, "the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree. I wasn’t pushed, I was inspired.”

And though the Annihilation actress could do without the interviews, red carpets and other public-facing parts of her career, she "always worked through parenthood," she noted. "It’s super important that you keep yourself intact."

The 46-year-old explained, "Work for me is a place where I feel inspired and I meet people—there’s that social aspect. Bringing that back home is a good thing for parenting—for me, at least."

And while Skarsgård still loves the "traveling circus" aspect of being an actor, he told Variety in February it's now time for him "to balance that with family life and making sure I can be present for my kid. I can’t be as selfish and narcissistic as I was before."

Because now he has a son to not push, but inspire, and let the apple fall where it may.

Read on for a guide to that huge Skarsgård family:

Born in Gothenburg, Sweden, on June 13, 1951, Stellan Skarsgård starting acting as a teenager in his home country, where he's long since reached national treasure status.

He's a familiar face in Hollywood thanks to films such as The Hunt for Red October, Good Will Hunting, Mamma Mia!, Thor, Dune and Sentimental Value, for which he won a 2026 Golden Globe for supporting actor, as well as roles on HBO's Chernobyl and Disney+'s Andor.

He married doctor My Skarsgård in 1975 and they had six children together—Alexander, Gustaf, Sam, Bill, Eija and Valter—before divorcing in 2007.

"My mom’s gone through a lot," son Bill Skarsgård told Esquire in 2024. "I’m very proud of who she is today. She’s devoted her life to help recovering alcoholics and addicts, which she’s gone through herself." (While largely a private person, My has talked about being in recovery and her work as an addiction counselor.)

Stellan and My welcomed their first child together on Aug. 25, 1976, in Stockholm.

"My dream was for my family to be normal and fit in and be like everybody else’s family," Alexander told Stellan in a 2025 sit-down for Variety. "For you to have a briefcase, that would’ve been fantastic, rather than a weird tote bag that you found in India."

Most people in our family are artists—a lot of eccentric, big personalities that I loved. But the early teens, bringing friends over was always like, 'Oh, God,' because I wanted it to be like everyone else’s household."

The actor known for True Blood, Big Little Lies, The Legend of Tarzan, Succession, Murderbot and more even joined the Swedish Navy at one point to distance himself from all the artistry—and the attention.

"Looking back, I don’t think it was an act of rebellion against you," he told Stellan. "But coming from a bohemian family, I was like, I want to find my own path. The most extreme contrast would be to go into the military. So it wasn’t a conscious 'F--k you, Dad” thing.

Alexander privately welcomed his first child with actress Tuva Novotny in 2023, but he's got time if he still wants to out-reproduce his father.

"My dad had kids in the ’70s, the ’80s, the ’90s, the 2000s and the 2010s," the Emmy winner told Chelsea Handler in 2013. And, he quipped, “I want to beat my dad."

While he splits his time between Sweden and New York, the Skarsgards remain "a very tight group,” Alexander told the New York Times in 2022. “Everyone lives within two blocks of each other in South Stockholm and we see each other all the time when I’m home.”

Gustaf was born Nov. 12, 1980, and started acting at 6, the first of his siblings to take the plunge.

“To any child, the first occupations that are presented to you are your parents’,” the Vikings and West World actor told Interview in 2017. “I was appealed to my dad’s occupation from the get-go.”

At the same time, he wanted to prove himself, turning down soap opera roles he was offered based on name recognition. "I was really pretentious in a sense," he recalled, "and was like, I’m going to drama school, to learn the craft. But in hindsight, I’m really grateful for that 17-year-old that got that early.”

Gustaf shares a daughter, born in 2020, with partner Caroline Sjöström.

Sam, born in 1982, picked up a few acting credits as a child but eventually followed in his mother's footsteps and became a doctor.

"He works at an ICU so he, on a daily basis, saves lives," Alexander said during a 2017 Interview chat with brother Bill.

Added Bill, "There's definitely a sense of embarrassment about what it is artists really do, at least for me in terms of acting. We have a mom and a brother who literally save lives."

Born Aug. 9, 1990, at first Bill wasn't too keen on "being number four," as he put it to Esquire in 2024 regarding his early trepidation about being an actor like his father and two older brothers.

But after breaking through in the U.S. in the series Hemlock Grove, then booking The Divergent Series: Allegiant, Atomic Blonde, It, Barbarian, John Wick: Chapter 4, Nosferatu, etc., fourth has started feeling like first.

Though he also sometimes fantasizes about a job that involves a briefcase—“Something more stable," he said—acting fit him like a glove.

"There are those moments,” Bill explained, “when you’re totally lost in the moment. When during the whole take you never thought once about the fact that you’re doing it. You aren’t acting.”

As for his own domestic life, the It: Welcome to Derry star welcomed a daughter with actress Alida Morberg in 2018 and confirmed in 2023 that they had welcomed her younger sibling.

Eija, Stellan's only daughter, was born in 1992 and works as a casting director for Swedish film and TV.

"During each of my wives' subsequent pregnancies, my daughter would say, 'I hope it's not a girl,'" Stellan told The Guardian in 2015. "She's very strong, stronger in many ways than the boys, and relishes her position."

Eija and husband Zeke Tastas welcomed son Aldous Judo Tastas Skarsgård in September 2025.

The youngest of Stellan and My's six children was born Oct. 25, 1995, and made his acting debut at 8 in the short film To Kill a Child, written and directed by Alexander. Around the same time, he played a younger version of Gustaf's character in the Swedish film Details.

Valter and Bill later played brothers in 2007's Arn: The Knight Templar, with Gustaf in the role of their father.

He's ventured beyond his family's business since, appearing in the horror films Don't Click and Funhouse, as well as the Netflix series The Playlist, about the founding of Spotify (a Swedish company, FYI), and the Canadian hockey series Börje.

Valter made his red carpet debut with girlfriend Melina Göransson in December 2024.

Stellan married wife Megan Everett-Skarsgård in 2009 and they have two children together.

Son Ossian was born April 26, 2009, and his first acting credit was providing the voice of "Young David" in the 2017 film The Wife. Through 2023 he was a regular on the Swedish fantasy series Trolltider - Legenden om Bergatrollet.

Born Aug. 24, 2012, Kolbjörn is the youngest actor in the family (for now), starring on the SVT horror series Blood Cruise. But while his older brothers experienced their own misgivings about taking up their dad's profession, nepo baby accusations have been particularly hard on the teen, according to his father.

"When his pals at school call him nepo baby, he gets so sad," Stellan told Vulture in 2025. "He gets isolated. Cruel kids—or cruel and ignorant. They love it on the internet. But it is such a bulls--t thing. Because nobody would hire you, at least not for anything good, if you’re not good enough."

So far, every Skarsgård that's ventured into acting has been good enough to get called back for more.

Stellan told Alexander during their Variety chat that, while he was pretty shocked when his eldest son joined the military, "I also knew that all you eight kids have different ways of approaching everything. Maybe I’m lazy, but I think it’s best to let you do it on your own."

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you're a math whiz.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#578. Emery's Villa 2.0 reboot restores optimism before Man City meeting

Aston Villa fans were in buoyant mood before the Champions League win against Viking at Villa Park

When Aston Villa walked out to face Viking in the Champions League, a giant tifo emblazoned with the message 'We've Conquered Before. We're Prepared For More' dropped down from Villa Park's famous Holte End.

At the same time, Villa manager Unai Emery was striding along the touchline to a standing ovation as he took the acclaim from supporters.

Emery celebrates the fourth anniversary of his appointment from Villarreal when Villa face Premier League leaders Manchester City at Villa Park on Saturday lunchtime, his arrival a transformative moment for one of the great old footballing institutions.

He has written his name into Villa Park history, adding to a track record there and at other clubs that marks him down as one of the game's elite operators.

And it was reflected in every moment against Viking with an emphatic victory.

Villa Park's mood was buoyant and expectant - restored to the state of optimism that came with last season's Europa League triumph following a campaign that saw 54-year-old Emery return the club to the Champions League.

It was in sharp contrast to some trepidation weeks earlier after a summer which saw a host of big names depart and Villa deliver what has become something of a trademark under Emery, a slow start that usually ends with the closure of the transfer window.

The scale of change at Villa can be underscored by the fact six of the starting line-up that won the Europa League with a 3-0 win against Freiburg in Istanbul in May left during the summer.

Norwegians Viking were duly dispatched 3-1 amid more jubilation, Villa making it three wins from three and actually topping the standings in the Champions League table until Peter Christiansen's late goal for the visitors left them level on nine points with holders Paris St-Germain, Liverpool, Real Madrid and Real Betis.

It followed on from the 6-0 win against Fenerbahce in the Champions League at Villa Park. Villa have now won 12 European home games in a row, under the great specialist Emery.

Little wonder, then, that Emery was elated as he looked ahead to Saturday's meeting with Manchester City, who have a 100% record from seven games.

Villa Park is certain to be high on excitement and emotion as Emery said: "Those three points fills us with confidence. We are comfortable, and of course as well getting balance, because after this match we are going to play against Barcelona, favourites, and then we play against Galatasaray away."

He also noted how Villa Park is right on board with his impressive transition into what can be described as "Villa 2.0", saying: "We now try to focus now on the Manchester City game on Saturday, hopefully the same atmosphere, the same energy. I am so, so happy but we must keep moving forward with the challenges we are going to face.

"There's still a lot of work to do, so how we are responding, getting better, is really fantastic."

Aston Villa manager Unai Emery - here celebrating a goal against Viking - has looked even more energised than usual in recent times

Emery, if it is possible, appeared even more animated than usual during the Viking game, looking energised by the renewal he had to perform in the summer and the promise shown by Villa's new players.

The list of summer departures looked daunting, with keeper Emiliano Martinez, Lucas Digne and Youri Tielemans leaving, along with England trio Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa and Morgan Rogers - the latter duo to Arsenal and Chelsea for a combined total of Â£172m as Villa raked in about Â£320m.

They had been integral to that Europa League win, the club's first European trophy for 44 years when they won the European Cup, and first domestic triumph since the League Cup win in 1996.

Villa's start to the season was slow, losing 4-0 at Brighton - with all four goals scored before half-time - then 1-0 at home to Arsenal. A goalless draw at Hull City was followed by 2-1 loss to Nottingham Forest at Villa Park.

The duck was broken with their first win at Spurs. Suddenly Villa and Emery looked like their old selves, culminating in those victories against Fenerbahce, a fine 1-0 win at Newcastle United, and Viking.

And what will please Emery and Villa's fans - who never wavered in their total faith in the manager they worship - is how the new signings have been contributing, suggesting the magician has produced a winning formula again, and quickly.

It will come as no surprise given Emery's back catalogue of work, which includes three successive Europa League wins with Sevilla, another with Villarreal and of course Villa's triumph. Even in what is regarded as an unrewarding spell at Arsenal, he still took them to the final of competition in 2019, although they lost to Chelsea.

It is why Villa's hierarchy, led by co-owner, Nassef Sawiris, give Emery everything he requires where possible.

Alongside sales, Villa spent Â£280m, and the early signs are they have invested wisely.

Unai Emery has lost six of the players that started the Europa League final win against Freiburg in May, including goalkeeper Emi Martinez

Against Viking, 20-year-old Brazilian Alysson, playing on the right flank, was Villa's most impressive performer. He preceded the summer signings, arriving from Gremio in January in a deal that could eventually be worth Â£10.4m.

He terrorised Viking with his pace, and even if his finishing still appears raw, he looks a superb prospect. Alysson won a penalty for Emiliano Buendia to put Villa two up, then ended a surging run by seeing his cross deflected into his own net by Henrik Heggheim for the third.

Ibrahim Mbaye, an 18-year-old signed in a Â£47m deal from Paris Saint-Germain, also showed flashed of rich promise on the other wing, a tantalising future partnership for Villa fans.

He appeared in all four of Senegal's matches at the 2026 World Cup, netting in a 3-1 defeat by France to become the youngest African player to score at a men's World Cup.

New keeper Zion Suzuki, the 24-year-old Japan keeper brought in from Parma for Â£30m, had big gloves to fill in replacing cult hero Martinez, but has looked assured, with the added bonus of an outstanding range of short and long passing that gives Villa an added dimension.

Joao Gomes, the midfielder in at Â£38m from Wolverhampton Wanderers, also showed what he offers against Viking.

Emery turned to a player who knew well to replace Watkins after he left to join Al-Hilal in the Saudi Pro League, signing Nicolas Jackson, who he coached at Villarreal, for Â£65m from Chelsea. He has settled quickly with five goals already.

Johan Manzambi, seen here celebrating his winner at Newcastle United, is one of a crop of exciting new Aston Villa signings

Arguably the most exciting arrival of all is Johan Manzambi, a break-out World Cup star with Switzerland. The 21-year-old midfielder cost a little more than Â£50m from Freiburg. It was a deal pulled out from under the noses of Newcastle United, leaving then manager Eddie Howe devastated.

He piled on the agony with the winner at St James' Park after scoring on his full debut in the victory at Spurs, although he is currently a doubt to face Manchester City.

Emery has not just made it a case of out with the old and in with the new as he rebuilds Villa.

Captain John McGinn remains the heartbeat of his side, while former England midfielder Ross Barkley is undergoing a late career renaissance.

The 32-year-old scored against Viking, his fourth this season, also scoring twice in the rout against Fenerbahce.

Barkley was a surprise signing from Luton Town in July 2024, having had a season on loan at Villa Park in the 2020-21 season.

Emery is a huge admirer and said after the win against Viking: "As a person, he is a fantastic guy. Ross Barkley is a very good player with experience, and his career, I don't know why, was going down after Chelsea.

"When we watched him at Luton, we thought, 'wow, what a player'. I am so happy with how he is playing, always being respectful whether he is playing or not. I am pushing him a lot offensively. I know he can score and can head the ball. I am very demanding of him offensively. I am happy for him."

It is in Emery's demanding nature to push his players a lot, although no harder than he pushes himself.

And it why those early concerns about how Villa would handle the departure of so many important, high-profile, players have been banished before Manchester City come to Villa Park.

#579. A Design Flaw in Share Links Exposes Users’ Personal Conversations With Meta’s Muse

Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.

Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:

“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”

In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: “We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.”

Asaf Aprozper, a cofounder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn but got no reply either way.

The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible.

“Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.”

Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended.

Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.

With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.

This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

#580. Fuerza Regida Wins Big at Billboard Latin Music Awards 2026: Complete List

The ceremony was broadcasted live on Telemundo from the James L. Knight Center in Miami.

Fuerza Regida was the big winner at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards on Thursday (Oct. 22), taking home eight awards including Top Latin Albums Artist of the Year, Duo or Group; Regional Mexican Artist of the Year, Duo or Group; and Regional Mexican Song of the Year for “Marlboro Rojo.” Additionally, the group received the Billboard Vanguard Award in recognition of a career defined by innovation and an unconventional creative vision that has pushed the boundaries of Mexican music.“We don’t have many words — there aren’t many words — but this represents a 10-year journey, a lot of hard work and a great deal of effort,” said the band’s leader, Jesús Ortiz Paz (JOP), upon accepting their special award. “We’re going to keep working, and we’re going to conquer the world, God willing.”

Although not present, Bad Bunny followed with seven Billboard Latin Music Awards, while Karol G, Peso Pluma and Romeo Santos won four each. Rosalía, Tito Double P and Prince Royce each took home three.

Rosalía, who was in attendance to receive the Billboard Hall of Fame Award, stated that she could not be an artist were it not for those who came before her — such as Celia Cruz, Rocío Dúrcal, Vicente Fernández, Daddy Yankee and Juan Luis Guerra, who presented her with the award. “It’s incredible to be receiving this today,” said the Spanish superstar, also thanking Latin America “for all these years of inspiration and lessons.” She also won awards for Latin Pop Artist of the Year, Solo; and Top Latin Pop Album of the Year for LUX.

The Billboard Latin Music Awards, broadcasted live on Telemundo and Peacock, featured 47 categories spanning major Latin music genres such as pop, tropical, Latin rhythm and regional Mexican. Additionally, for the first time fans had a historic opportunity to choose one of the night’s winners through a new award, Fan Favorite Artist, which went to Karol G.

Among the artists set to perform throughout the evening are Carlos Rivera, Chuyin, Elvis Crespo, Erick Brian, Ha*Ash, Jessi Uribe, Kapo, La Nueva Ola de la Cumbia, Manuel Turizo, Melymel, Nanpa Básico, Nella, Ozuna, Pablo Alborán, Paola Jara, Pututi & Nesty, RIZA, SANTOS BRAVOS, Tito Double P, Víctor Manuelle, Xavi and Yahritza y Su Esencia. For a full list of performances, click here.

The ceremony also honored Cristian Castro with the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award for his enduring and exceptional career; and Rubén Blades with the Billboard Icon Award, celebrating his timeless career in Latin music.

#581. Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue

Citing problems with the data transmission network, Italian authorities have drastically reduced the volume of flights in their airspace. The ENAV authority ruled out malicious activity and said flights remained safe.

Air travelers across Italy faced delays and cancellations on Friday because of a problem with the country's air traffic control systems.

The ENAV air traffic control authority ruled out foul play such as a cyberattack, and said it was forced to introduce temporary restrictions of the volume of flights after identifying a data transmission problem.

Major airports in cities like Rome and Milan warned of likely disruptions and advised passengers to check with their airlines.

ENAV said it first identified the issue overnight. It was forced to restrict the volume of flights at around 6 a.m. (0400 GMT/UTC) as the number of scheduled services increased.

"We would like to inform you that this morning we guaranteed the greatest possible number of departures, including intercontinental flights," ENAV said.

Shorter-distance services were more likely to be interrupted.

"Despite the anomalies encountered on the data transmission network, we are deploying all available resources to minimize disruption and restore full operations as soon as possible," ENAV said. "We confirm an operational capacity of 50% of total air traffic, ensuring maximum safety at all times, which remains the Company's top priority."

ENAV said it had ruled out the possibility of the disturbance being caused by "malicious acts."

Rome airports operator ADR warned passengers that "flight delays and cancellations may occur" and advised passengers to contact their airline if uncertain. Milan airports company SEA issued a similar notice.

#582. Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage’s polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4–6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

It details the fabrication and measurement of single-molecule Au-helicene-Au junctions and presents experimental analyses of their operation as molecular machines, together with control experiments and a discussion of alternative explanations for the observed effects. It also includes density functional theory calculations of the molecular junction structure and rotational potential landscape, as well as quantum electronic transport calculations. Finally, it presents a microscopic theoretical framework that explains the current-induced torque, molecular rotation, and current enhancement underlying the observed behaviour.

Stochastic jump of the molecular rotor from one potential minimum to the next, driven by fluctuations and current-induced torque. Here, the work done by friction exceeds the work done by the current-induced torque. The molecular junction video is based on density functional theory calculations of snapshot configurations at different rotation angles.

Free rotation of the molecular rotor along the tilted potential, driven by fluctuations and current-induced torque. Here, the work done by the current-induced torque is greater than that done by friction. The molecular junction video is based on density functional theory calculations of snapshot configurations at different rotation angles.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you stick your nose where it doesn't belong.

Strands, the New York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

If you're feeling stuck or just don't have 10 or more minutes to figure out today's puzzle, we've got all the NYT Strands hints for today's puzzle you need to progress at your preferred pace.

#585. Infantino re-election hopes boosted by Asia support

Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (left) had previously criticised Gianni Infantino over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme

Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president have been given a major boost by an endorsement from the head of the Asian Football Confederation.

President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa told the confederation's Congress in Tokyo - which was attended by Infantino - that "we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you as you seek a new mandate as president".

Sheikh Salman's backing represents a significant u-turn just two months after he signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf criticising Infantino over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

At the time the three confederations accused him of breaking trust "through deception" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, and "a profound failure of judgement...these are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership."

But in what appears to be a blow to the rebellion against Infantino, Sheikh Salman told the meeting in Japan it was time "to move forward".

"I've spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear," he added.

"Yes, we had some issues, we spoke about them in the past, but let's not relate the two things together...

"As one Asian family, we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni."

Alongside Infantino's power base in Africa and South America, Sheikh Salman's endorsement could be crucial in ensuring the Fifa president secures a fourth and final term.

At the election in Rabat in March, Uefa will have 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.

Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents

Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency?

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.

Potential rivals such as Victor Montagliani, the president of Concacaf, and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders.

"You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my dear Salman," Infantino said in an address to the confederation's delegates.

"You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years."

Asked later about Sheikh Salman's comments, Infantino said: "I feel great about the AFC's support."

At a meeting of Fifa's Council last week, Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan, but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised.

He also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (Â£2.6bn).

Uefa has since told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by 2 November.

#586. Apple iPhone Duo Review: Is It Worth It?

It’s a little hard to review the iPhone Duo. I’ve been toting Apple’s first folding smartphone for the past week, and several apps I’ve tried to open on the sprawling 7.6-inch screen look awful. Thick, black bars on the sides, with a phone-sized app in the middle of this tablet-like display. But you likely won’t encounter this problem once the Duo is in your hands.

In the past day, a handful of apps I use regularly updated to add full support for the iPhone Duo’s screen sizes and vertical user interface elements. Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.

Developers need to target the iOS 27.1 software development kit (SDK) for full Duo compatibility. That will take some time. But it is a little maddening that some app developers, who for years have never seemed to care about optimizing their app for Android folding phones, are so quick to embrace Apple’s fold. Slack, for example, never offered the two-pane view of its desktop app in the Android version, but it’s on the Duo. C’est la vie. Hopefully, Apple’s entry into foldables will result in a “rising tide lifts all boats” situation and Android fold lovers will get to enjoy those optimizations.

The iPhone Duo’s Standby mode turns on when the phone is propped up via a kickstand.

The iPhone Duo arrives seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold. In Apple tradition, its first entry into an existing category feels fully mature; the Duo has significantly less jank than the first few generations of its Android counterparts. The infamous crease—where the phone folds—is hardly visible thanks to Apple’s display stack and clever use of a matte-finish nanotexture screen. The phone is IP68 dust- and water-resistant (though avoid taking the Duo to the beach, as sand is notoriously detrimental to phone hinges). The software experience, barring the unoptimized apps, feels carefully considered.

Apple has also landed on the right shape, months after Samsung realized it following seven years of narrow, somewhat awkward book-like folds. The wider, shorter “passport” design feels better than what’s come before in this category. The 5.4-inch outer screen is still big enough to be useful, and the hinge glides open gracefully and stays put at various angles. The hardware feels polished.

That’s not to say Apple has completely trounced the competition. I still appreciate that Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold8 is super lightweight at 201 grams, as the iPhone Duo’s hefty 254 grams (heavier than an iPhone 18 Pro Max) can get tiring after extended doomscrolling. I don’t love the fact that, when closed, one side of the Duo has angled corners and the other is curved—the Fold8 looks better in that regard. Touch ID also takes a little getting used to after years of relying on Face ID, mostly when you’re holding the Duo with your left hand and you suddenly have to authenticate an app or purchase with your right hand. (It can mercifully auto-unlock if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.)

Apple also tightly controls the multitasking experience. If you have two apps split-screen on the Duo, Apple won’t let you resize one app to be slightly bigger than the other like you can on Android. Here, a 50-50 split is always enforced. You can’t add a floating third app when in split-screen either, even though Apple has offered a similar capability on iPads for years. (The exception is video apps—you can have them float in picture-in-picture mode.) In portrait orientation, you can split-screen only with a video app; Apple won’t let you stack two apps, something Android has enabled for years.

That rigid software philosophy extends to basic input handling, too. I am typing this review on the iPhone Duo using a compact folding keyboard with a tiny attached trackpad. The trackpad works OK, but I could only get it to work after turning on AssistiveTouch in iOS’ accessibility settings. If the Duo is the iPhone that lets you do more, Apple should natively enable cursor support just like it does on iPads.

Then there are the physical quirks. The Duo supports MagSafe, so you can magnetically stick the phone to MagSafe tripods, mounts, and the like. (When it’s open, the Duo’s weight makes the phone sag to one side.) But what about MagSafe wallets? They’ll work, but Apple’s official wallet sticks out past the phone’s lower edge—not what you’d expect from a company that pores over every detail. Apple doesn’t have an official solution, so you’ll have to rely on a third-party accessory (and I suspect there will be many Duo accessories).

The iPhone maker follows the industry standard with a dual rear-camera system, lacking the third zoom camera from its Pro iPhones, which I sorely miss. At least the selfie cameras—the one on the outer screen and the “hidden” under-display inner camera seem to produce good results. On a Zoom call, my editor remarked that the video quality looked “really good” with both selfie shooters. (Zoom, by the way, wasn’t optimized.)

When an app is properly optimized, the experience is chef’s kiss. Multi-pane views let you see a lot more in an app than candy-bar phones, a boost to productivity. Split-screening two optimized apps looks excellent, with plenty of room for each app to breathe and let you multitask. I haven’t found myself putting the Duo in angled positions much, mostly because I’ve really enjoyed using it with Apple’s Folio With Kickstand case, so much so that I wish the kickstand were integrated into the phone itself; I strongly recommend investing in an accessory to prop the Duo up.

Battery life has been pretty great. With average use, I’ve ended most days with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Right now, with over six hours of screen-on time because I’ve been working off the Duo for most of the workday, it’s almost 6 pm, and I’m at 45 percent. Impressive.

As for performance, the only thing I've noticed is the Duo can get toasty. This isn't necessarily tied to a demanding task, though. Half an hour in Battlefleet Duo or Pokémon Go didn't make the phone feel much warmer (though 15 minutes in Ungodly did), but at random moments, the right half of the Duo heated up quickly. It's something to keep an eye on.

Duo Preview lets the photo subject see themselves in the frame.

The dual rear cameras are reliable, too. You don’t get the fun variable-aperture wizardry of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera, but after comparing photos I’ve captured on both devices, the results aren’t drastically different. That brings us to the features I think will help bring folding phones into mainstream appeal—Smart Take and Duo Preview.

The latter is a staple of folding phones, letting you show the camera’s viewfinder to the photo subject—good news for anyone who has ever complained about their Instagram husband. Now you can make sure they’re angling the camera just right before hitting the shutter button. You can also take better-quality selfies with the rear camera yourself— open the camera app on the larger screen and flip the phone; you’ll get an option to view the camera controls on the outer screen, letting you see a live preview while snapping with the superior 48-megapixel cameras.

Smart Take is similar to Google’s Magic Capture. Set the phone down in a partially folded shape (so it looks like a tiny laptop) and tap the shutter button. The camera will then wait for you to get into position and snap a series of photos when it thinks you’re posing. You can forget about asking someone to take a picture for you. It’s not as smart as the Pixel feature—I ended up deleting a bunch of awkward Smart Take photos—but it’s convenient.

I’m sure Kids Cue will be popular too. I don’t have a kid, so I couldn’t vet how well it works, but it loops cute Snoopy animations on the outer display to capture a child’s attention and make them smile. Google and Samsung have similar versions on their folding phones, but neither has Snoopy—a big win for Apple.

The nanotexture finish on the inner screen is the star of the show. The matte surface reduces the crease’s visibility, while also minimizing glare and reflections. It also feels like e-paper, which I imagine will be very welcome when Apple Pencil support is added later this year (via a software update). Writing on a screen always feels better when the screen isn’t entirely smooth.

You don’t get the crisp video quality, deep blacks, and sharp contrast of the iPhone 18 Pro when watching movies and shows on apps like Netflix on the nanotexture panel. However, colors are still just as vibrant, and the experience is very similar. I didn’t have any issues with screen brightness—the Duo gets up to 3,000 nits at peak outdoor brightness—even with the textured finish, though off-axis viewing isn’t great in direct sunlight.

Much of my time this past week has been thinking about wasted space. Sometimes I questioned Apple’s decision to move all the navigation elements of iOS to the right rail—there’s so much wasted space in some apps! Then I use an app that uses all that space, and I’m content. That’s probably my takeaway. If you want to try Apple’s first folding phone, wait a few months for developers to optimize their apps. (It might actually help that the phone is backordered until January.) Waiting might help in other ways too—Apple plans to add Reachability later this year for the Duo, letting folks with small hands more easily access the left or right edges of the screen with a tap.

You’ll likely spend most of your time on the outer screen of the Duo.

This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues but because I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.

Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but, on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).

But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.

#587. LISA’s ‘Press Play’: All 6 Tracks Ranked

The global diva returns, relaxed and razor-sharp. Hit play, and a six-scene movie unfolds in your ears and behind your eyes.

On Sept. 27, LISA took home best pop at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards for “Dream,” beating a field that included Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Rodrigo, and becoming the first K-pop soloist to win the category. It added to a run that already included a No. 7 peak on the Billboard 200 with last year’s Alter Ego. Then in September came pre-release single “SaWaDiKa,” which entered the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 69.

Now, with that momentum behind her, LISA unveils her new EP, Press Play. The title comes from a line on “Tarantino”: “It’s a movie baby, come and press play.” It’s a fitting name for a record that hits the eyes as hard as the ears. Press play and the scenes flash by: a tuk-tuk weaving through the streets of Bangkok, a Ferrari tearing around a circuit, a dance floor after midnight, a motel straight out of a Tarantino film, a yoga studio.

LISA holds a songwriting credit on every track, and Kuk Harrell, the vocal producer behind Rihanna’s “Umbrella,” worked on vocal production. Rap and sing-rap dominate much of the record, but each track carries its own texture, so it never drags.

The world should get ready for the movie LISA has brought with her. Below, Billboard Korea ranks all six tracks on Press Play.

“Cut U Off” opens with one of cinema’s most famous whistles: the tune Elle Driver whistles as she walks down a hospital corridor in a nurse’s uniform, on her way to kill the Bride in Quentin Tarantino’s Kill Bill: Vol. 1 (2003). Paired with LISA’s blade-sharp opening bars (“Chop chop,” “Master of sashimi”), it makes for a thrilling, suspenseful start.

LISA reframes the thrill of revenge at the heart of Kill Bill as the satisfaction of cutting someone off for good, delivering every line cool and unbothered. Past that striking intro, though, the track settles into easy-listening territory and doesn’t quite sustain the tension it opens with. Still, it’s a solid album cut that does its job.

Picture doing yoga while floating in zero gravity, following LISA’s every cue, and you have “Sweat,” a dreamy, otherworldly track. Each time her loose but bouncy “Stretch it out,” “Don’t stress me out” lands in your ear, your body loosens one beat at a time. Even as the stretching cues repeat rhythmically, she keeps varying her flow, so the song stays engaging to the end. A playful, flirtatious streak (“Now make me your muse”) hums underneath, so the track never feels flat.

And when LISA, who has already declared “Yoga is my antidote,” finally offers “Inhale, exhale,” a wave of relief washes in. Whatever reality you’re living, it’s OK to pause and catch your breath. It plays like the end credits of a movie that’s been racing at full speed.

This is where the EP’s world-building is most explicit. “Got my nails really long like the barrel of my gun,” LISA opens, a witty first line that instantly turns her glamorous manicure into a prop from a Tarantino film.

Over sound effects that evoke a swinging blade, she calls up the director’s filmography one reference after another: Kill Bill, Death Proof, a katana, even “Hollywood in your hands.” “Mustard all on my sneakers” summons the Bride’s yellow tracksuit, while “black suit” conjures his sharp-dressed gangsters. It’s a song you hear but also see. And slipping some Thai flavor into the mix (“At the drive-thru Thai funk shaking out the trunk”) is pure LISA.

Production comes from two Dutch-born producers. Thom Bridges, who also produced “SaWaDiKa,” is a dance music veteran who worked on Yellow Claw’s Blood for Mercy, a No. 1 on Billboard’s Dance/Electronic Albums chart, and has collaborated with David Guetta and Steve Aoki. He’s joined by Beau Nox, who co-wrote and co-produced five tracks on Drake’s Honestly, Nevermind, including “Falling Back.” A Tarantino world built by producers who’ve spent years lighting up clubs is enticing before you even hit play. The song gave the EP its name, but for sheer ear-grabbing power, “V12” edges it out.

“V12” is full of twists. LISA opens by murmuring the syllable “Sa,” in a mood that’s at once reverent and laced with her signature mischief. In Thai, “sa” can mean “bold” or “sharp,” and in the Isan dialect it can mean “widely talked about.” Just as you start savoring those layers, she flips the sound to “Sike” (as in “psych”) and turns the mood on its head.

As “Sa” and “Sike” trade places, a thudding beat and a low voice announcing “V12” slowly build the anticipation. When LISA finally arrives, she’s relaxed and commanding. As she raps at an unhurried pace, the line between her and the V12 engine, the beating heart of a high-performance supercar, starts to blur. Obsessive attention to detail, like 12 cylinders machined to mesh perfectly (“Devil in the details”), without chasing perfection itself (“I don’t chase perfection”). A rarity you can’t buy off the shelf (“Couldn’t cop this at retail”). Overwhelming power at full throttle. The V12 engine is LISA herself, which is why “You should be impressed” doesn’t sound like a boast.

The track is produced by Dem Jointz, who worked on Dr. Dre’s Compton and is familiar to K-pop fans through his work with NCT 127, among others. Listening feels like riding shotgun in the indigo Ferrari she brags about on “SaWaDiKa,” leaning back as she takes a slow lap around the track.

“Dance / floor / Tempo / Fast / Slow / Go.” A hook built from single words tossed out one at a time couldn’t be simpler, and that’s exactly what makes it clever. One listen and your body starts counting the beat on its own. The melodies are smooth throughout, and the pre-chorus (“Hold up / This place about to go up”) instantly raises the temperature in the club. A sound that wails like an ambulance siren adds a fresh twist. The scene writes itself: 10 after midnight, LISA speeding to the party in a matte black truck, because, as she puts it, “the party don’t start till we roll up.” Produced by Johnny Goldstein, the track interpolates Missy Elliott and Timbaland’s 2003 “Bomb Intro/Pass That Dutch,” pulling in the air of an early-2000s hip-hop club. “Tequila mixed with soda / Got me moving like a cobra.” It’s a track that makes you want to twist like a cobra and dance along.

The undisputed No. 1. The confidence that made it the pre-release single runs through every second. Assured rapping and vocals lock together, and the “Hello Sawadika” hook is irresistible enough to charm the whole world. “La la Lisa la diva / Sawadika there she go.” Has there ever been a cleaner self-introduction?

Just as striking is how boldly she wears her Thai identity. On the second verse, LISA shouts “Bang bang Bangkok bang” and yells “geng mak,” Thai for “so good,” with her crew. Baht piling up in the bank, donuts in a tuk-tuk: the heart of Bangkok unfolds in full color. Mid-song, the repeated questions “How many got discipline / How many that been where I been” call to mind the road she has traveled from a girl in Buriram, Thailand, to global diva.

Thom Bridges and Ojivolta produced the track. Ojivolta, the New York duo who won the Grammy for best rap song with Kanye West’s “Jail” and helped craft hits for The Weeknd and Justin Bieber, also have BLACKPINK ties: they co-wrote and co-produced ROSÉ’s “On the Ground” and “BADGRRRL” from LISA’s Alter Ego. With Ojivolta back in the fold, already well versed in her strengths, the result is a fearless greeting. It’s the movie’s opening sequence, and the song that best sums up the EP.

#588. Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter

She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser. Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.

Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.

Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," said cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."

Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."

"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," noted Weltz-Rombach.

Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.

After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, said Weltz-Rombach. That the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books, she added.

Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.

In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," said Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance."

The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.

Since Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explained Weltz-Rombach.

"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

"[Women's] resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," said Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." Other examples include a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters.

Even though many of the eyewitnesses are now dead, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."

#589. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#591. Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power

Bournemouth have beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now AC Milan in the Europa League

At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation.

That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture.

Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final.

Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008, not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts.

"It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports.

"So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special."

To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two).

While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point.

In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A.

The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years.

For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare?

Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance?

Bournemouth sweep aside 10-man Milan in Europa League

English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once.

In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them.

In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them.

Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21.

The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams.

But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years.

So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory?

Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List.

It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League.

Premier League clubs earn more than Â£1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined.

Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30.

Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'.

Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final.

In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively.

In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League.

All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates.

The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of Â£3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues.

Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight.

You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings.

Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent.

"With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August.

"A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer."

'That was for the fans who were going when we were facing liquidation'

Despite the success of Premier League sides in the Europa League and Conference League, the Champions League is a harder nut to crack.

While Barcelona, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich all lost to English teams in last season's elongated Champions League league stage, it has been a very different story when it really mattered.

Over the past two campaigns, eight of nine English teams have been knocked out by one of the Deloitte Money League's big four, according to the last report produced in January 2026.

Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Liverpool were eliminated by an aggregate score of 25-6 last season.

No English club appeared in the top four of Deloitte's Money List, with Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain leading the way. Three of those have won the Champions League five times between them in the last seven years.

English clubs are certainly very much in the mix for the Champions League, with Arsenal losing last season's final on penalties and Manchester City winning in 2023.

But, with just one English club in the past three finals, the Premier League elite are yet to take their European domination to the very top.

Come May, it could well be Bournemouth, Brighton, Crystal Palace or Sunderland leading the English charge in Europe.

#592. Tom Skerritt Dead at 93: Costar Julia Roberts Pays Tribute

After Tom Skerritt’s family confirmed Oct. 22 that the Picket Fences actor died of natural causes at the age of 93, former costars like Julia Roberts and Kathy Baker paid tribute.

Tom Skerritt is being fondly remembered by his family and friends.

The film and TV actor, known for his roles in hits like Top Gun and M*A*S*H, died Oct. 21 of natural causes, according to his family. He was 93.

“We are heartbroken by his loss,” the family shared in a statement to People. “While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives.”

The statement added, “He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices.”

While Skerritt’s family asked for privacy amid his death, they noted they were “incredibly grateful” for the wave of “love and support” shown by his friends and former costars.

Indeed, Julia Roberts—who earned her first Oscar nomination after starring as Skerritt’s onscreen daughter in the 1989 film Steel Magnolias—shared a still image of the pair in the movie on Instagram, writing in the caption, “A shining light of a gentle man. RIP.”

His Picket Fences costar Kathy Baker also remembered the Emmy winner, who she called her “darling friend.”

“My heart is broken to hear of the passing of dear, lovely, loving, Tom,” she shared in a statement to People. “He taught me so much during our four years on Picket Fences. I couldn’t have asked for a more gracious and kind actor to work with, and it was very special to share with him the incredible run of the show.”

Meanwhile, their Picket Fences colleague Lauren Holly—who played Deputy Sheriff Maxine Stewart under Skerritt’s Sheriff Jimmy Brock—noted she “adored” her former costar.

“He was our leader,” she wrote on Instagram. “His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much. He cared deeply for his family—both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet, and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life, and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter.”

Holly concluded, “Rest easy my friend. I will think of you often.”
