#593. Best Gifts for Mom (2026): Digital Wall Calendars, Better Bags, Personalized Jewelry, and More

Moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day, her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving. The holiday season is right around the corner, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.

If you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin to the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device, moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these are items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs. Or they might be at the top of my own wish list as a mother of a 4-year-old.

Updated October 2026: I've added new gifts to this guide, including Nora Fleming stoneware, jewelry from Gorjana and BaubleBar, Rumpl’s Gametime Puffy Blanket, The Zero Proof's Pampered Pregnancy Pack, and Mina Baie's Emmy Diaper Bag, and have ensured up-to-date links and prices.

The must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin. HigherDose is a favorite mask of mine because the three-strap design lets it hang on my head rather than squeeze it, making it one of the most comfortable masks I've worn.

My other favorite LED tool actually sits on my head and also comes from HigherDose. The brand's Red Light Hat treats your head with red light to rejuvenate your scalp and hair follicles for better hair growth, and as someone with a sensitive scalp and a hair-pulling problem, using this cap regularly genuinely improved my scalp and hair. It's the healthiest it's ever been, and my scalp is the least itchy, too. I love that this hat also has a battery pack, so I can comfortably wear it anywhere while I treat my head.

Look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

The Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a stylish personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.

If your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.

My latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar. These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can quickly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa. The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device. You can also gift her kiddo a Skylight Buddy ($140) so that she doesn't have to remind them to check the main calendar for their chores; it'll appear on their own device if they have a Buddy.

If Mom loves entertaining—or just being festive—but doesn’t want to have to store a million different dishes, Nora Fleming’s modular serving-tray system is for her. First, pick a base—there are trays, baking dishes, utensil crocks, and even salt and pepper shakers. Then, pick one of dozens of hand-painted “Minis,” or ceramic accents (sold separately). There are holiday themes, sports team themes, and even ones for specific events like mah-jongg or BBQs.

Each base has a hole into which you can attach the Mini with a little rubber stopper. I tested the cracker tray with a harvest-themed Mini, and you wouldn’t know the tray didn’t come with the accent already attached. At the end of next month, I plan to swap it out for a Christmas tree Mini, and so on. Best part is that if Mom likes this setup, you’ll be set on gifts for the foreseeable future, provided you can keep finding new Minis you think she’ll like. —Kat Merck

For years, the go-to gift for a woman in my family, mother or not, was shopping in the jewelry section of a department store. My mom even helped orchestrate this for the rest of the aunties and grandmas, but now, as a mom myself, I find myself interested in jewelry that tells a story about my family and children instead of just any old set. (Except extra earrings for my earring stack, a gift I'm thrilled to get, because there's never enough.)

I love these pieces from Gorjana and BaubleBar that you can customize. Gorjana has a ton of charms you can add to its necklaces or bracelets to reflect Mom’s kids’ initials, birthstones, or anything else; I paired a charm of my son’s first initial ($48) with the Wilshire Adjustable Necklace ($65). If she's more of a ring gal, BaubleBar's Toi et Moi ring ($78) lets you choose two birthstones to display. I chose my and my son's birthstones, but luckily his sibling-to-be will also have a red birthstone, so it'll remain a perfect reflection of my kids and me for years to come.

This item was literally made for sports moms: a padded stadium cushion with a wearable blanket inside. My son plays on three sports teams, so I do a lot of sitting outside on bleachers and turf sidelines—and often at night, when it’s freezing. I’ve tried many things to keep warm, from heated jackets to HotHands, but nothing has worked as well as this water-resistant blanket, which unfurls to 50 x 70 inches and sports a clip at the front so you can wear it like a cape. It can also be used for picnics or as a spot for younger siblings to sit and read during tournaments. It’s also not hard to fold it back up and fit it inside the seat part (which is 1 inch thick without the blanket inside). It comes in six colors, so you can be sure to find one that matches your giftee’s kid’s team or school colors. —Kat Merck

If a mom in your life is exploring her nonalcoholic drink options, The Zero Proof has some gift sets perfect to give so she can try out several things at once. I'm currently grounded from drinking any cocktails while I'm pregnant, but moms (and people in general) can have all kinds of reasons to want to explore unique, interesting drinks that are sans alcohol. I really liked this set for how many cool drinks it exposed me to, from bottles of nonalcoholic wine to knockoff cocktails. If you're looking to spend a little less, my favorites so far have been the Château del Ish Non-Alcoholic Sparkling Espumante ($20) and Lapo's Non-Alcoholic Melograno Mule ($20 for four).

Look, I love a Kindle, but if you want to get the best e-reader for your buck (or maybe she just wants an e-reader that isn't a Kindle), the answer is actually a Kobo. My favorite is the Kobo Libra Colour. It's cheaper than the Kindle Colorsoft and can also double as a digital notebook if you add on the $70 stylus. I also prefer Kobo's annotating options: You can write right on the pages instead of in weird pop-up margins and boxes only on Kindle. Kobo also has a page-turner remote ($34), which I love to pair with a pillow stand holder so I can lean back and relax without holding up my e-reader while I read. I gave a similar pillow stand to my mom, and now I can spot her last reading spot easily because that pillow is resting there.

You could also gift her one of the new Kindles if she's a Kindle addict. Many of my friends are drooling over the new purple Ube color of the 12th-gen Kindle ($149), but my personal favorite is the Kindle Aluminum (I just wish it were cheaper!). There's also finally going to be a Kindle page-turn remote, the Kindle Click ($35).

I love a backpack when I'm on the move with my 4-year-old, but one thing that annoys me is that things are hard to find inside, because packs are typically so deep. That's why I adore the Mina Baie Emmy Diaper Bag: It's a wide, shallow bag instead of a long one, making it easy to open and see most of what I store in it without digging around. I'm not toting diapers at the moment, but I've used it to pack a ton of snacks, toys, and spare clothing for my kid.

I'm intrigued to see how using it with two kids goes—I chose the Emmy Midi, which is the midsize bag, but if you're a pumping parent or need to carry a ton of bottles with formula, you might want to try the larger Emmy Full. The stylish bag is made of vegan leather and can be converted from crossbody to tote to backpack mode, depending on which straps you use. Mina Baie doesn't include a changing kit, but sells one separately ($59) if you'd like to include it in your gift (or buy that as the gift to upgrade their existing bag of choice).

I'm expecting again, and this time I'm on a mission to find a good pregnancy pillow. I tried a large body pillow on the advice of another site for my first pregnancy, and it was honestly an awful experience—the pillow was too large and firm for me to comfortably use, let alone have room for both it and my growing midsection in my bed. Plus, it was heavy, which is annoying when your body already feels too cumbersome to move around.

So far, using the Wildbird Pregnancy Pillow has been the opposite. It's slim and light with just enough squish to add a little support under or around my belly without being difficult to get comfortable. It’s beautiful and easy to maneuver around. Wildbird also suggests it for other support positions postpartum, and I'm curious if those will work for me. But it makes for a beautiful gift for any expecting mom and will be one she's excited to put on her bed and curl up with at night.

Once my kiddo is asleep, you can find me parked on the couch playing video games. I upgraded to a Nintendo Switch 2 ($499) earlier this summer so I could finally buy and play Pokopia ($70), since it's exclusive to the new console, and I already can't wait to use it to play the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ($60) remake coming out in November. It's also quickly become an experience I can share with my son now that he's 4; he's been helping me and my husband replay Tears of the Kingdom, but he mostly requests we help him build monster-hunting robots and cook food for Link like he's a starving Tamagotchi.

If you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another big update in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam users and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big plans to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games if she already got herself the new gadget like I did.

For most moms, showers are sacred—especially for moms of babies or younger kids. However, heavy metals, sediments, chlorine, and PFAS can cause health problems not just in drinking water but in water that touches the skin, as well. They can also cause buildup on hair and shower surfaces, making them harder to clean. Many municipalities—including mine—treat water with chlorine, and when I asked him which filter he'd recommend for my own shower, former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage suggested the Weddell Duo. It's the only US filter he's found that has certification for chlorine and lead removal from NSF International, and it also cites third-party testing by IAPMO R&T showing it can remove PFAS, though there's no corresponding certification.

Still, the Duo has a 2.5-gallon-per-minute flow rate and can remove most chlorine from over 8,000 gallons' worth of showers. It's an in-line filter, so it's easy to install in minutes—just screw it in between your pipe and showerhead. It even comes with a little roll of waterproof tape to ensure a leak-free fit, and because of the horizontal orientation, installation won't affect the showerhead height. The filter needs to be replaced every three months, but refills only run about $25 each, compared with competitors like Filterbaby or Rorra, which can cost $40 to $45. —Kat Merck

As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons.

I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight and the Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

If you know a mom who loves to bird-watch (I know one!), you can upgrade her bird feeder to a smart one. Smart bird feeders add a camera to the feeder so she can see a close-up feed of the birds that come to hang out in her yard, and they're adorable to boot, for a little smart curb appeal. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck recommends the original Birdfy feeder as a great gift; it's her favorite smart bird feeder and comes in adorable colors to brighten your mom's yard and catch the eye of neighborhood birds. But the one she and I both have our eye on (her for her mother, me for myself) is the Birdfy Nest Duo, which is actually a birdhouse with two cameras so you can see the birds entering the nest outside and raising a family inside.

There's a wellness gadget for everything now. Rings that track your sleep and blood oxygen levels, masks to make you look younger, massagers to relax your muscles, and now boots to improve circulation. WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane says her mom loves these compression boots from Therabody to improve circulation, which is a common problem for many of our aging parents. These boots combine compression, vibration, and LED therapy into a single wearable device that comes with eight preset routines to focus on legs, knees, and joints. It's a unique option if she wants better recovery for her legs or better circulation for her health.

The DeLonghi Rivelia is the best and easiest and most user-friendly superautomatic espresso machine I have tested. What’s superautomatic mean? It means you pour whole beans into the hopper, put milk in the milk carafe, and select the drink you want to make on the touchscreen menu. Then you let the machine do most of the rest. The style of espresso made by a superautomatic machine like this Rivelia is generally a bit smoother and less intense than the sort you get in a café. But the process is also less finicky; you won’t be dealing with coffee grounds and portafilters. What’s especially nice with this Rivelia is the ability to make multiple “profiles” for different coffee drinkers in the house, each with their own favorite drinks—and the ability to swap out bean hoppers to make decaf coffee in the afternoon. The Rivelia is also the machine my own mother, a drinker of lattes and dark-roast beans, loves unreservedly. Like others on the WIRED Reviews team, I often ask colleagues and those close to me to test my top-rated machines over long periods to see how they hold up over months or years of regular use. My mother thanks me nearly every month for letting her test the Rivelia. —Matthew Korfhage

Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night."

Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared..

In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork?

This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting.

So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more.

"When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com.

But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? In short, "we analyzed the painting astronomically, analyzed documents about his situation in July 1889, and then carried out ecological and meteorological investigations," Kim said.

To start with, the team analyzed the sky from the exact location in Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh is said to have painted "The Starry Night." They then used observational geometry to map the historical night sky.

"Modern telescopes are equipped with a function called astrometry, which compares an image of the night sky with celestial coordinates stored in a computer and automatically extracts the coordinates of the image," Kim said. "We used Procrustes analysis, a method that compares only the 'shape' of two sets of points. After matching their position, size and rotation, it measures how similar the two shapes are from the differences that remain (the residuals)."

"Because a star cluster on the canvas may be larger or smaller than in reality and slightly tilted, this method was the right fit. It allowed us to explain, in quantitative terms, what earlier studies had described only qualitatively as 'resembling a certain constellation,'" Kim added.

But this quantitative analysis wasn't enough to say for sure that this was the right-fitting sky, as different constellations could fit to a similar degree, Kim explained. To get closer to their answer, the team combined their analysis with a deep dive through history.

"We also checked whether the stars were actually in that part of the pre-dawn sky on that date, whether they fall within the painter’s field of view, and whether the appearance of the moon and Venus matches the painting. It was the Hyades that satisfied all of these conditions," Kim said.

As mentioned, the date of this matching sky comes in late July, a month after art historians think Van Gogh painted "The Starry Night." But the researchers suggest that their findings could provide evidence to support the idea that the work was actually painted in July.

Letters written by Van Gogh as early as 1888 describe his desire to paint a star-filled sky. A letter dated April 12, 1888 reads: "A starry sky, for example, well — it’s a thing that I’d like to try to do, just as in the daytime I’ll try to paint a green meadow studded with dandelions."

Kim followed these letters through the months to try and find more information that could potentially alleviate the discrepancy between the matching skies and the actual month the painting was created. Kim pointed to a letter from between late May and early June 1889 that reads: "This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big."

Kim drew on "personal imagination" to find ties between Van Gogh's sky observations in these months and what they might mean for the painting's timeline, Kim shared, so this doesn't definitively change the view of this painting's history. However, Kim suggested that these records could indicate that Van Gogh was repeatedly looking up and watching the pre-dawn sky, which could have led to him seeing this exact sky on July 22.

The painting itself even ignites uncertainty among art historians. As the researchers cite in their new paper, leading art historians see "The Starry Night" as stylistically different from Van Gogh's other works during the month of June, drawing further questions over the date painted.

"What our study shows is that the sky in the painting matches, in both observation and shape, the real pre-dawn sky around July 22. So, what we propose is the possibility that Vincent conceived the idea in June and completed the painting after July 22," Kim said.

However, "I think further research in art history and conservation science could shed more light on this question," Kim added.

This work was described in a study published Oct. 22 in the journal Scientific Reports.

#595. Wilcox wants Howe if Carrick sacked; Hürzeler has ‘no time’ for United rumours; Dortmund fight the influencers: football – live

⚽ All the latest news going into the weekend’s action ⚽ Premier League: weekend guide | Mail Tom

Some Ligue 1 news amid the ongoing unrest in France, the fixture between Paris Saint ⁠Germain and Olympique ​Lyon has been pushed ⁠back to Monday evening from ⁠its original scheduled ​date ‌of Sunday ‌night. LFP added that its decision ‌followed an order from the ​Paris police department, which had earlier raised ⁠concerns the match could ​be ​a security ​risk, as ​the French capital ‌braces for ​another ​weekend of protests.

Antonio Conte has released a statement on his Instagram story denying reports linking him with an immediate return to management. Without naming Manchester United, the Italian says he is not in ‘advanced negotiations’ with any club and any reports of demands on wages or terms are ‘unfounded’.

double quotation markFollowing recent media reports in Italy and abroad, I feel it is appropriate to clarify my position.

My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage. Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right.

I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my “strong personality”. These reports are unfounded, as there is currently no concrete basis for such assessments.

Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties’ needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager.

Until then, any assumptions about my demands and my professional future remain speculation and cannot be treated as fact.

Brighton head coach Fabian Hurzeler insists he remains fully focused on his own job and has the utmost respect for the work “great human being” Michael Carrick is doing at Manchester United.

A humiliating 4-1 loss away to Como in the Champions League on Wednesday night and the criticism from captain Bruno Fernandes which followed has put further scrutiny on Carrick’s position.

Following the Seagulls’ fine start to the new campaign, Hurzeler is one of the names touted as a possible replacement for Carrick at Old Trafford should the club decide to make another managerial change.

The German coach, though, maintains he is only thinking about how to keep Brighton moving forward into this weekend’s game at Liverpool, with his side held to a goalless draw in the Conference League away to Czech minnows Jablonec on Thursday night.

“I am really focused on my job here,” Hurzeler said at a press conference. “I have no time to think about these rumours because we play every three days.

“Beside that, I have a lot of respect for Michael Carrick, for what he has done with Manchester United at the end of last season. He is a great human being, he is a great personality. Every time we meet each other, we have a really good relationship, so therefore I really respect him and there is nothing more to say about that.” Press Association

Most footballers like to spend their summers unwinding after a long season but not Pascal Gross. Having been part of the Germany squad eliminated in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024, the midfielder entered – and won – a running race.

Gross completed the 8.4km course on Juist, in the East Frisian islands, in 31 minutes and 35 seconds. He is not known as someone who courts attention, and his victory by more than a minute came to light only when a video was posted on social media by a competitor.

Gross was moving from Brighton to Borussia Dortmund after seven years in the Premier League and reported to his boyhood club for pre-season training days later. Running is an obsession for Gross, as it is for his former teammate James Milner, who revealed last month he was training for a marathon after finally hanging up his boots, and that has shown since he returned for a second spell at the Amex in January for a bargain £1.2m.

Read Ed Aarons’ feature on Brighton’s hard-working midfielder:

A stadium selfie could soon cost fans of German giants Borussia Dortmund after the club announced plans to reward those who leave their phones alone during the game.

Dortmund are offering signed jerseys and gift cards for club merchandise to fans who use an app which measures how often they unlock their phones at its stadium. Arguing that “more and more fans are annoyed by selfies, streaming, and social media in the stands,” Dortmund say supporters can opt to use a “fan mode” in the club’s app, starting Saturday with a home game against Eintracht Frankfurt. The rewards scheme and app are entirely voluntary and there’s no ban on fans using their phones.

Fan mode will measure how often the phone is unlocked during the game — not counting the halftime break — and award points to people based on how little they use the device, with prizes on offer for those with the most points. Each time the phone is unlocked, the user loses points.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” said Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer.

The club’s stance is part of a backlash in German football against attempts to turn its stadium atmosphere into social media content, especially by influencers using professional camera equipment.

Hertha Berlin said this month it was banning “commercially produced and monetized” video productions from its games, while allowing fans to take photos and videos for personal use.

Another club, Dynamo Dresden, said in August it would ban commercial filming for social media, saying it wanted to ensure fans felt comfortable at the game and to protect the club’s TV rights deals. Agence France-Presse

The ongoing security situation in Saudi Arabia makes it ⁠difficult for the country to host next year’s Asian Cup as scheduled, according to Tsuneyasu ​Miyamoto, president of the Japanese ⁠Football Association.

Several major sporting events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled or ⁠postponed amid escalating attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, raising doubts over whether the continental soccer ⁠tournament can take place as scheduled in January and February ‌next year.

“Based on ‌what I’ve learnt from the news, the situation is ‌still unsafe, so at this point, I don’t think it would be easy to hold the AFC (Asian) Cup there,” Miyamoto told reporters at the Asian Football Confederation’s (AFC) extraordinary congress in Tokyo.

“I just had a meeting ‌with the Saudi side and they said that their top priority is the safety ​of the players, the fans, and everyone who would be attending the tournament.

“They said they would work with the AFC to decide whether the tournament can go ahead, ⁠so they did mention that it would take ​some time (to ​make that decision).“

AFC ​chief Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa said last ​week a ‌postponement until 2028 ​remained ​a possibility if necessary, but the local organising committee later said it was sticking to the original schedule. Reuters

Frank Lampard has been talking about Frank Lampard’s Coventry ahead of the Sky Blues early-season basement battle with Fulham. Namely, Lampard has been talking up the work ethic of Gus Hamer after the 29-year-old rejoined Coventry from Sheffield United in the summer for a reported £6million.

So far, fan-favourite Hamer been restricted to four appearances off the bench on his return to the Premier League. Following his latest cameo role in Monday night’s 3-1 defeat at Tottenham, Hamer asked to play for the under-21s on Tuesday lunch-time and Lampard was impressed. “He wanted to play. It was a personal decision and I like that,” Lampard said at his pre-match press conference. “He wanted to play and get minutes because Gus has been used to playing minutes regularly, pretty much.

“And these days at Coventry from his days at Sheffield United we’ve got a competitive squad now and his area of the pitch is competitive.

“But Gus has been very, very good to work with since he’s come back to us. Myself and my staff have been really, really impressed by his approach, his training, his ethic and what he wants to do. And Gus is going to help us.

“We all know, everyone in the building and at the CBS knows that he’s a really talented player who’s going to help us. So he’s just staying ready, and I’m very pleased with how Gus has been. He’s a good example.”

Hello, happy Friday. Have we had football every day this week? I think we have… Monday night football, three nights of European games and now Friday night at Portman Road. What a world.

Right, that’s my stint done. Time to hand over to Tom Bassam for the next wee while. Bye.

“Surely the most popular request for Uniteds new stadium will be ‘seats facing the other way’?” honks Tim Woods. I have to say, as a stadium nerd and stadium aesthete, that were I given a vote I’d opt to mothball the whole thing as it’s quite the ugliest new arena design I’ve seen in a while.

Álvaro Arbeloa’s been talking ahead of Fulham’s trip to Coventry on Saturday, and buoyed up by last weekend’s much needed win over Hull. “Nothing has changed for us,” insisted the manager, “we were not winning games but we believed in ourselves, we were doing so many things well,

“The most important thing [about the Hull win] is we were in same situation against Manchester United and Ipswich but didn’t win but now we had to improve in our transition and did. We controlled the ball in their half better than before.”

As for that first win lifting pressure off him, Arbeloa said: “It’s not about me, it’s about my players and the supporters because they were behind us and the players because of the work they’ve done.”

In Spain, it’s the Clásico on Sunday at the Camp Nou, with leaders Barcelona having made the better start to the season, though Real Madrid – six points behind – have begun to hit their straps. But is it still the world’s biggest match? Here’s Graham Ruthven:

double quotation markAs the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture?

Sunday’s match at Camp Nou will be watched by hundreds of millions of viewers all over the world. A clásico always carries significance, but this weekend’s edition will be especially significant. A Barça win would move them nine points clear of their rivals at the top of La Liga. A Real Madrid victory could be a catalyst for the rest of their season.

At the risk of sucking all the air out of the room with more Manchester United chat, Marco Rose has inevitably been asked for his two pennorth given his Bournemouth side visit Old Trafford on Sunday. And he reckons his buoyant side will face “angry and intense” opponents. “I’m quite sure [Michael Carrick] will tell his players it’s all about mentality, effort and attitude,” said Rose. “You hear all the voices and noises but I don’t know it helps us and it’s up to us to go there and be focused, react well. They’re going to be angry and intense and we have to face it.”

Three games ago we were talking about Bournemouth possibly having a bit of a hangover season – and they’re still lowly placed in the Premier League – but they’re pretty perky right now.

Manchester United are inviting fans to offer their views via a survey on the design of the proposed new 100,000-seat stadium.

Colette Roche, United’s CEO New Stadium Development, said: “Our proposed new stadium is one of the most significant projects Manchester United will undertake in the next 100 years, and it is vital that we shape it together with our fans. Above all else, this is a football stadium built for them, so getting the details right matters.”

Supporters have until 6 November to take the survey, with subjects including: “creating a world-class football stadium and match-day experience for all fans”; “heritage and legacy”; “atmosphere”; “the wider campus”; and “getting to and from the stadium.”

The survey will be sent to season ticket holders, cup season ticket holders, executive club members, official members, supporters who have purchased hospitality at Old Trafford within the past three years and season ticket waiting list members, a press release stated.

It’s north London derby day in the Women’s Super League tomorrow, with Arsenal arriving at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium under considerable pressure after their poor start. Derby passions will run high with Spurs’ Cathinka Tandberg, for one, bang up for it, as she explains in this interview with Sophie Downey:

double quotation mark“It means more than just three points. It’s for the whole club. It’s for the whole place. It’s for the whole of Tottenham.” One only needs to be in the presence of Tottenham Hotspur’s Cathinka Tandberg for a few minutes to feel the passion that emanates from her when it comes to this weekend’s north London derby. As a lifelong Spurs fan, the forward understands more than most the intensity of the rivalry that exists between her side and Arsenal, one that she cannot wait to experience once again on Saturday.

“It will just be an incredible feeling,” she tells Moving the Goalposts. “I think you will feel a few nerves that you maybe don’t feel in a normal game but that’s good.”

“All the Spurs fans hate Arsenal and Arsenal hate Spurs. That’s how it is. You want to show that you’re the best team. Simple as that. You just want to fight for the club, the badge and for the people around you.”

double quotation markThe noise continues. Eddie Howe is the under-fire Jason Wilcox’s choice as next cab off the rank should Michael Carrick be binned. Jamie Jackson has all the latest:

Eddie Howe is the current preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox to replace Michael Carrick should Manchester United decide to change manager, with the director of football believing Howe’s extensive Premier League experience places him ahead of other potential targets.

Howe left Newcastle in late July to take a break from the game but would seriously consider a return for the United role, it is understood, should this be offered.

In Manchester City on-field news, Erling Haaland is back fit to face Aston Villa at Villa Park tomorrow, PA reports. The Norway striker was not risked in City’s Champions League victory over AEK Athens in midweek after a blow to the foot in the previous game against Ipswich.

City will continue to assess Nico O’Reilly, Mateo Kovacic and Matheus Nunes, who also suffered knocks in the same game. The manager, Enzo Maresca, said: “They could all be available or not. There are still doubts. Erling is the only one who is 100 per cent available and for the other three we need to wait.”

Jonathan Liew’s column on how Brazil’s footballing and political dysfunction feed each other is a good read:

double quotation markWe hear a lot about football’s power to unite a nation. Perhaps we underestimate the extent to which it can also divide; the way it can reflect the very worst of ourselves, our greed and vindictiveness, our lust for feuds and, petty entertainment. There is a Women’s World Cup being hosted in Brazil next summer and while Lula has sought to fast-track the professionalisation of women’s football, Bolsonaro’s only public utterances in the field of women’s sport have been to assert his opposition to trans athletes playing it.

In courage of their convictions news, the Asian Football Confederation has decided to endorse Gianni Infantino’s Fifa presidential re-election bid.

The AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, speaking at the body’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement.

“We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the Fifa president.” Sheikh Salman said. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well.”

Morning everyone. What about them Cherries eh? Before we dive deep into weekend previews, Manchester United melodramas and what have you, some moments to reflect on last night’s action. Chief among them was the continuation of Bournemouth’s European fairytale – a deserved 3-0 Europa League shellacking of Milan, a result barely conceivable two decades ago, but, as Nick Ames sagely points out in his match report, not a great surprise given the resources even mid-ranking Premier League clubs can now command compared to fading Serie A giants.

Elsewhere, Sunderland dug in for a draw at Lech Poznan, Crystal Palace’s mixed start to Europa League life continued in a 2-2 draw at Besiktas, and … oh Celtic. A third European defeat on the spin for Martin O’Neill’s side as they surrendered a 1-0 lead to lose the Celt derby 2-1 to Celta Vigo, who brought 3,000 fans to Glasgow – reportedly their biggest ever European away turnout – for a cultural love-in.

Anyway, we’ll have pre-match news, interviews and comment through the day, and feel free to mail in your thoughts. Off to a game this weekend? Tell us your hopes for it. In the meantime, to get in the mood, here’s 10 English top-flight things to look out for.

#596. EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China

At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation.

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."

Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.

The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.

Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.

Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.

"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.

"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.

Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.

As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.

The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.

Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.

"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.

"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.

"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

#598. Sutton's predictions v Waffle the Wonder Dog and his owner, Simon

Manchester City have won their first seven Premier League games of the season but will their 100% record survive Saturday's trip to an improving Aston Villa side?

"Villa have beaten City in this fixture in each of the past three years under Unai Emery," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"They will fancy it this time too - they are seven unbeaten in all competitions, and flying at the moment."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week eight, he takes on Waffle the Wonder Dog and his owner Simon, who is played by actor James Merry.

Waffle's After School Club, featuring James and Waffle, is available on CBeebies and BBC iPlayer right now, with lots of fun after-school adventures for families to enjoy together.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Waffle's After School Club often ends in mayhem and mess despite the best efforts of Simon. How will the pair get on at predictions?

Waffle is a talking dog whose adventures on his show often end in chaos for Simon and the rest of his family.

Like most dogs, he loves football - or at least loves chasing one.

"I am an enthusiastic baller," Waffle told BBC Sport. "But technically my best position is right-back... on the sofa.

"My favourite player is the England captain, Harry Kane-9, and I'm a Liverpool fan so my all-time hero is Kenny Dog-leash.

"My fur is red and I am a poodle so of course I support the Reds, or Liverpoodle as I like to call them - they never walkies alone."

Waffle loves watching Liverpool on Match of the Day. "It's past my bedtime on a Saturday night, so instead I like to watch them on iPlayer after an early Sunday morning garden wee."

In real life, actor James Merry is an Aston Villa fan, who has a long connection with the club.

"I grew up in Sutton Coldfield, north Birmingham, and just about everyone is Villa there," he told BBC Sport.

"My mum's side of the family are all fans - my great-aunt was a season-ticket holder for about 40 years and my nan lived most of her life on Witton Road, which is just round the corner from Villa Park.

"My first job was there too - when I was 16 I worked in the catering department serving burgers on matchdays.

"Then, during the summer I had to clean every executive box and polish all the cutlery and make sure everywhere was properly stocked.

"We had the run of Villa Park and I was like a kid in a candy shop."

Chris Sutton, Waffle the Wonder Dog and James Merry were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

So, I am up against a talking dog this week? I'm not sure that improves my chances of winning - I've been barking up the wrong tree with my predictions all season anyway.

One of us has got to beat AI though - I've been reading about it in the news and it is not just with football scores where it seems to be taking over.

This game is a tough one to call, though. It is going to be very tight.

Nottingham Forest can't score. That's their issue, and they have only managed five goals in their first seven league games.

It did make me laugh when I read that Forest boss Oliver Glasner had got Chris Wood to give advice to the other strikers about finishing - why not just play Wood then?

Ipswich are still bottom of the league table based on my predictions (see bottom of page) but they ran Manchester City close in the end last week and are doing better than everyone expected, myself included.

I like what Tractor Boys boss Gary O'Neil is doing there, and they already have three league wins from seven games - the last time they were in the Premier League, in 2024-25, they only managed four all season.

Forest are second bottom and could really do with getting something here, and Ipswich haven't drawn a game yet - so that's what I am going for.

James' prediction: The director of Waffle, Tim Hopewell, is a Forest fan and I have gone for them here. I like the way they play. 1-2

Villa have hit a bit of form and seem to be getting back to the level they were at last season.

They had another good win in the Champions League this week, but then you'd expect them to beat Viking pretty comfortably.

Emery's side played well against Newcastle last week too but I thought Newcastle were a bit too gung-ho, and paid the price. City are a lot more streetwise.

City are going to slip up eventually this season but the fact they have lost on their past three visits to Villa Park actually makes me think it will be different this time.

Erling Haaland is fit too, which will obviously help. With all the heat on the club at the moment it could just turn out to be one of those seasons where they continue on this incredible run.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: Ross BARKley gets two for Villa, but Erling HOWLand to score a hat-trick. Sorry, dad! 2-3

James' favourite Villa players: The early to mid-'90s was the time when I was getting into football so Dean Saunders and Dalian Atkinson were my heroes, and Paul McGrath as well. That was certainly a golden era - I need to mention Shaun Teale too, because he was always a favourite. I think I had his name on the back of a shirt.

Now? I think most people of my generation would pick John McGinn. He is an absolute club legend for what he has done for us down the years and my shirt now has got McGinn on the back.

James on Villa's season: We seem to be picking up some form after another slow start. It looks like Johan Manzambi is going to be pivotal for us this season and Nicolas Jackson has started well, he has stuck a few away.

This might sound a bit bonkers but, with Emery's record in Europe, I am more excited about that than what we might do domestically, because I think we might go deep in the Champions League.

James' prediction: Because we are weak at the back at the moment I think City will score two or three, but we are looking lively up front and could do the same. I've got to be partisan - and I am also going to go for a barnstormer. 3-2

Arsenal were so ugly in the way they beat Nottingham Forest last weekend, but were a lot easier on the eye in the midweek draw with Bayern Munich.

They are going to be without the injured Bukayo Saka for this game, but they are at home and they should still have too much for Everton.

Everton will make it tough for them, of course, but I am not sure how they will hurt the Gunners.

James' prediction: Arsenal are just a machine at home. 3-1

Whoever loses this is likely to end the day in the relegation zone.

Sometimes these kind of games can be quite cagey, with both teams afraid of being beaten, but here I feel like Coventry and Fulham will have a go and there could be a few goals flying in.

Coventry have a bit about them going forward, especially when they use their pace on the counter-attack, but they are also a bit vulnerable defensively.

Because of that, I am going to go with Fulham. They got their first win of the season against Hull last week and they are definitely capable of getting another one here.

James' prediction: My old man is a Coventry fan - he was born and bred in Cov but then married a Brummie and moved to Birmingham so he was always on a hiding to nothing trying to get me to support Coventry. He won't be happy because I've gone for a draw here. 1-1

We were talking on the Monday Night Club about what Chelsea could do this season without any European football.

Tottenham are not in Europe either, of course, but they don't look like they are going to be challenging at the top of the table the way Xabi Alonso's side are.

People keep saying how Chelsea's attack is so good, but their 2-0 win over Everton last time out was their first clean sheet of their campaign in the league, and that side of thing still needs to improve.

Spurs, meanwhile, do seem to be getting better, albeit slowly.

It was a big result for them to beat Coventry on Monday but they have an awful record at Stamford Bridge, with only one win there in the Premier League era.

I don't see them getting anything this time, either.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: Archie GrayHOUND will score a couple for Spurs, but I'm backing Chelsea because I was a fan of Didier DOGba back in the day. 4-2

James' prediction: Chelsea carry so much attacking threat. 3-1

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage's future appears to be in some doubt but his critics seem to have forgotten that they are 14th in the table, when the Eagles finished 15th last season under Oliver Glasner.

Yes, Palace had a heavy defeat at Brighton last week and it doesn't help it was at the hands of their big rivals, but it is not like Sage has got one point from his first seven games. They are leaking a few goals, but there are reasons for that.

There has been huge change at Selhurst Park in recent months, with some key players leaving, especially at the back. Others have stayed but are still unhappy, and Sage has had a lot to contend with.

Palace play in Turkey on Thursday night which won't help their preparation for this game, but I still feel like they will get something against Newcastle.

There has been a lot of change at the Magpies too, but the thing that worries me most about Matthias Jaissle's side is that they are so open.

'Chaotic' was the word I used to describe them against Aston Villa last week.

Villa are always very well structured in the way they play but they got chances against Newcastle just by persevering with their build-up play.

If Newcastle don't get their press quite right again here, then Palace will cause them problems too - I definitely don't see this game as being one where defences are on top.

James' prediction: Both teams will be happy just to get a point on the board. 1-1

Although Hull have made a great start I still think they will get relegated.

We know they will have a go at Brentford, but the Bees will be too smart for them.

Brentford would have beaten Liverpool last week without Yehor Yarmoliuk's stupid red card. If they can keep 11 men on the pitch, they will win this one.

James' prediction: Brentford are such an amazingly well-run club with what they have achieved. They are going to be too strong for Hull. 1-2

Liverpool have an extra 48 hours to prepare for this game - they played Villarreal at home on Tuesday, while Brighton are away in the Czech Republic on Thursday.

I don't think it will make any difference, though, because the way that the Seagulls play, I am expecting them to go to Anfield and win.

This has the makings of a great game but, while Liverpool have had a couple of good results, I am still not convinced by them.

Andoni Iraola's side are a work in progress with a tendency to empty their midfield and that means Brighton can hurt them.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: A win for the Liverpoodles! 2-1

James' prediction: This is going to be close. Brighton are playing really well but I am still going to back Liverpool at Anfield. 2-1

After all the stick I got from Manchester United fans for saying they would get thumped by Leeds last weekend, it turns out I was only a few days out - it happened against Como instead.

United have been poor all season, though. That's why I went for them to be despatched like that - the 5-0 scoreline was a little bit tongue in cheek, but the point I was making has been proven this week.

The Bruno Fernandes criticism of Michael Carrick just adds to the problems United have at the moment - it is as if they are at the stage now where you have to pick who you want to back.

I don't know where United go from here but I am going for a Bournemouth win - the Cherries will attack them, and their great recent record at Old Trafford will give them confidence too.

If United do lose, I think it will be the end for Carrick because I just don't see how he survives this.

Even if United get something from this game, it is still just a matter of time before he goes.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: BARKus Rashford to win this for United. 2-1

James' prediction: Carrick really needs a win and they are at home so I think he will get it. 2-0

Sunderland have killed me this season because I just don't seem to be able to predict them at all.

The Black Cats are bottom of the table after losing four league games in a row and their boss Regis le Bris has a few problems to solve.

One of them is having European football that stretches their squad - they are away in Poland on Thursday - but at least they will have striker Brian Brobbey back from injury at the weekend.

After last weekend's loss at Bournemouth, Sunderland defender Nordi Mukiele suggested the Black Cats may have become "arrogant", but I don't see that outburst being as damaging as the ones by Manchester United players recently.

Still, things like that are better kept inside the dressing room because some of Mukiele's team-mates will be asking him if he was calling them arrogant.

I was never arrogant as a player, by the way, but people used to call me far worse than that in my day.

Maybe we will see a reaction from Sunderland here, but I still don't see them winning this because Leeds are battle-hardened and are a good team too.

They weren't at their best against Manchester United but still picked up a point, and they won't be leaving the Stadium of Light empty-handed.

Waffle the Wonder Dog's prediction: I like the sound of LEADS United and I love playing with George the cat (who lives next door) but 11 Black Cats means it's hide-behind-the-sofa time! 0-2

James' prediction: I had a look at all the fixtures and I thought one of them has got to finish 0-0, hasn't it? I have gone for this one. 0-0

#599. De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

#600. Anna Faris' Mom Costar Defends Her After Chuck Lorre's Criticism

Mom alum French Stewart praised costar Anna Faris for their time working together on the Chuck Lorre sitcom following the producer's comments about the actress' reputation in his memoir.

French Stewart still considers Anna Faris like family.

That's why the Mom star, who played Faris' overzealous boss on the CBS sitcom for seven seasons, defended her on social media following series creator Chuck Lorre's less than flattering comments about the actress in his memoir.

"I was disheartened to see Chuck Lorre throw her under the television bus in his new book," Stewart penned on Instagram Oct. 21. "I’ll say this. Whenever I saw Anna—I saw a woman working hard to make a good show."

Stewart applauded the Scary Movie alum as one of his "all time favorite costars" who "delivered on show night." And the actor is no stranger to a TV set, given his work on ensemble comedies like 3rd Rock From the Sun, The Middle and The Horrible Terrible Misadventures of David Atkins.

"The vast majority of my eight years on Mom was spent working with Anna," Stewart continued. "She was Mom. The spine of the show. And a legit good person."

In addition to witnessing the House Bunny actress' comedic chops, Stewart also worked alongside Allison Janney, who starred as Faris' mom, and Jaime Pressly, who played their friend, socialite Jill Kendall.

For Stewart, Faris was always "Funny. Kind. Prepared." But his review of working with Lorre—who hinted that Mom's cancellation was tied to Faris departing "for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show"—wasn't as glowing.

"Whenever I saw Chuck—I saw a man trying hard not to turn into a werewolf," the 62-year-old wrote. "That was my experience. I wouldn’t trade a day working with her."

Pressly too spoke highly of her run with the female-led cast.

"I just really thoroughly enjoyed being able to go to work with girlfriends every day," she exclusively told E! News. "All of us of a certain age, it was nice. It was refreshing."

And the Hot Chick actress isn't the only one who left a hit production while it was still on air. Read on for other stars who exited popular TV shows.

Gregg Sulkin, Wizards Beyond Waverly Place

In the Wizards of Waverly Place spinoff's shocking series finale, Selena Gomez's Alex Russo reunited with teen love Mason Greyback (Sulkin)—only to reveal a devastating twist.

#601. Gaming Can’t Afford More Games the Size of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’

Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives in November. A staggering 13 years and two console generations after the release of its predecessor, the long-awaited sequel has effectively become one of gaming’s holy grails—a title that some thought they’d never actually see, its development cycle so legendarily long that there’s a dedicated “we got [x] before GTA 6” meme.

The latest criminal opus lets players control Jason and Lucia, a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, and bears all the hallmarks of Rockstar's incredible attention to detail. Leonida, the open-world setting based on Florida, looks almost impossibly vast yet meticulously detailed, with its own weather systems and hundreds of animal species roaming around.

It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing.

At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is. On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade. Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition).

Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online. With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game.

Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them.

The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis. It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios. Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches.

Take 2025’s Battlefield 6 as an example. Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation. A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though).

It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch.

With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback. Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”)

Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games. It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns.

However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience. Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost. Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine­—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay.

The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways. Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer. But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments.

Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2? Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it?

The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller.

That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles. In short, rediscover the “AA”-scale game.

The textbook example of how successful this can be is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded. The RPG earned rapturous reviews and endless fan acclaim, celebrated for its challenging dodge-and-parry twist on turn-based combat, its stunning world—a breathtaking blend of belle epoque and dark fantasy imagery, wrapped in a gorgeous painterly flourish—and its mature and emotionally complex story of explorers battling the inevitability of death.

In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either. Clair Obscur has motion-capture performances, a voice cast featuring Hollywood heavyweights like Charlie Cox and Andy Serkis, a full orchestral score, and dazzling visuals. It even packs a solid 60-odd hours of playtime, making it feel significant and not daunting. It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026.

While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff. The game was hugely successful for its budget, letting the studio continue without resorting to painful layoffs. Sandfall’s success isn’t a one-off. Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences.

Another major benefit of aiming smaller is that it lets companies mitigate rising development costs for themselves and consumers. The memory crisis is forcibly extending the hardware life cycle, delaying new console generations and blocking supplies of powerful PC graphics cards, leaving many players without the means to reap the benefits of the most demanding games.

As Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi—no stranger to hugely ambitious games with incredibly long development cycles—says, “There isn't a single console that you can say, ‘As long as I have this, I'll be able to play everything, to do everything.’ Personally, I think that over the course of the next 10 years, if someone said, ‘Here's the next generation of consoles,’ the market and the audience are not necessarily going to just jump over.”

Hamaguchi says the industry will still straddle the lower-spec options, like a Steam Deck or Nintendo Switch 2, providing broader experiences to a wider base. It won't be so much about cutting-edge technology, but how developers can compete in game design. "I think we're going to be entering an age where that's really the focus of competition,” he says.

Sadly, this approach has one big problem: Developers are already trying it but failing to draw investment. There’s no easy answer—investors follow the money, and the money points to GTA-scale games, even though AAA development increasingly leaves carnage in its wake.

Even Rockstar appears to realize the current approach is unsustainable, with studio veteran Phil Hooker telling Bloomberg that “the engine, the tools, and the team we've built during the [GTA VI] project will allow us to do things more quickly” in the future. Hopefully, good news for fans who fear another decade-long wait for GTA VII.

Grand Theft Auto VI will be a success, and its longevity is already certain. But when every other publisher sees the inevitable slate of sales records the game will shatter, they’d do well to think twice before chasing it—the games industry might not survive if they do.
