#634. Christopher Lloyd Marks 88th B-Day With Perfect Post on "Serious S--t"

Christopher Lloyd celebrated his 88th birthday by revisiting Back to the Future 41 years after the iconic film's release. Plus, he shouted out his fans and family, including his wife Lisa Loiacono.

Christopher Lloyd has life down to a science.

The sci-fi movie legend who starred in 1985's Back to the Future didn't need a flux capacitor or plutonium to solve the equation about what matters most to him on his 88th birthday.

"Today I turn 88…I’ve seen some serious s--t," Lloyd mused on X on Oct. 22. "The most serious of it all is love."

Indeed, the Addams Family star couldn't help but call back to his unforgettable role as Doc Emmet Brown in the time travel trilogy, in which he told Michael J. Fox's character Marty McFly, "If my calculations are correct, when this baby hits 88 miles per hour, you're gonna see some serious sh--t."

And while he's maintained an illustrious career from movie sets to Broadway stages for over 65 years thanks to his 1.21 gigawatts of star power, Lloyd has cherished his relationships above all else.

"I love my family, my friends and my wonderful fans," the Who Framed Roger Rabbit villain continued. "The power of love remains."

Lloyd's family includes real estate agent Lisa Loiacono, whom he married in 2016 after first meeting when she helped the One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest alum sell his home.

Of course, fans of the actor—who has starred in countless genre classics including Star Trek III: The Search for Spock, My Favorite Martian and Clue, alongside Tim Curry—showed heavy-duty admiration in response to his birthday post.

"Tough to believe I can reply directly to Christopher Lloyd in this day and age to directly wish him a Happy Birthday and thank him," one user replied on X, adding, "Happy Birthday, Doc. You made my childhood better."

Time travel to the Back to the Future set with these behind-the-scenes secrets of how the movie was made.

1. Writer and producer Bob Gale came up with the idea for Back to the Future while looking through his father's high school yearbooks during a visit with family and discovering his dad was the president of his graduating class. As he put it to Esquire, "I wondered whether I would have been friends with my dad in high school."

2. For years, multiple studios passed on the script, more than 40 rejections in total. Among them: Disney, with Gale claiming they said, "Are you guys out of your minds? You can't make a movie like this here. This is Disney, and you're giving us a movie about incest!"

3. Not a fan of the title, Universal Pictures head Sid Sheinberg suggested the name be changed to Spaceman From Pluto.

4. John Cusack and Johnny Depp originally auditioned for the role of Marty McFly, but C. Thomas Howell was the finalist for the role, ultimately losing out to Eric Stoltz.

5. Five weeks into filming, the filmmakers realized Stoltz wasn't the right fit for the role, with Gale explaining to The Guardian, "The humor just hadn't been coming through with Eric. The studio weren't happy exactly, but they'd seen the footage so they bit the bullet."

6. Director Robert Zemeckis was the one to deliver the news to Stoltz, with the filmmaker recalling in the book Blockbuster that it was "the hardest meeting I've ever had in my life and it was all my fault. I broke his heart."

7. Reshooting all of the scenes Stoltz had already filmed added a reported $4 million to the movie's budget.

8. Because Michael J. Fox was the original first choice for Marty, the filmmakers worked with the team at his hit sitcom Family Ties to make sure they could have him as their leading man. "We would've danced naked on his desk to get Michael J. Fox, so of course we said, 'Yeah, sure, we'll adjust our shooting schedule,'" Gale told The Hundreds blog.

9. Fox's filming schedule was intense: He would shoot Family Ties during the day and then go right to the Back to the Future set from 6:30 p.m. to 2:30 a.m., averaging five hours of sleep a night. "It was my dream to be in the film and television business, although I didn't know I'd be in them simultaneously," Fox said during a TV special. "It was just this weird ride and I got on."

10. There is one scene with Stoltz still in the film. Though you can't see his face, it's Stoltz who punches Tom Wilson's Biff at the diner.

11. In the original script, Doc Brown was called Professor Brown, with a studio executive recommending the change.

12. Jeff Goldblum auditioned for the role of Doc Brown, according to Gale, who said, "The only other guy we really seriously considered for Doc Brown was Jeff Goldblum. Jeff came in, and…I'm certain we talked about John Lithgow, but I don't remember if he ever actually came in, or if we met him. But I vividly remember meeting Jeff and liking him."

13. Christopher Lloyd almost passed on the iconic role, hoping to do a play in New York instead. But he credited his wife, Carol, who "reminded me that I always told myself never to turn anything down without at least checking it out."

14. In an interview with the Seattle Times, Lloyd revealed his two inspirations for Doc: Albert Einstein and Philadelphia orchestra conductor Leopold Stokowski, who had white hair.

15. One of the reasons for Doc's hunched over stance? To help with the seven-inch height difference between the two leads.

16. The Office's Melora Hardin initially snagged the role of Marty's girlfriend Jennifer, but was recast before she even began filming after Fox replaced Stoltz. The issue: At 5-foot-5, she was an inch taller than Fox.

17. Though Claudia Wells originally played Jennifer in the first film, she retired from acting after her mother was diagnosed with cancer. Elisabeth Shue took over the role for the remaining installments.

18. Originally, the studio was hoping Doc's car would be a Ford Mustang, with the company paying for the placement, but Gale refused, telling AdWeek, "I said, 'No, no, no, Doc Brown doesn't drive a f--king Mustang.' It had to be a DeLorean."

19. Huey Lewis, who wrote the hit songs "The Power of Love," and "Back in Time" for the film, makes a cameo as one of the judges in the band audition.

20. Lewis originally declined to work on music for the movie when he was approached by the director.

21. In an early draft, the time machine was set to be a refrigerator, but Zemeckis was worried children would accidentally lock themselves in refrigerators, so it was changed to a car.

22. Originally slated to open in August 1985, test audiences reacted so positively to the movie that the studio moved the release date up. Back to the Future hit theaters nine weeks after completing production.

23. Crispin Glover, who played Marty's father George McFy, didn't return for the sequels due to contract disputes. He later filed a lawsuit after filmmakers used footage from the first film and put a mold of his face on another actor "in order to fool audiences into thinking I was in the movie," he said on The Opie and Anthony Show.

Ultimately, a settlement was reached, with The Hollywood Reporter detailing that he received $760,000 at the behest of the company that insured Universal.

24. Lea Thompson credits her turn in 1984's The Wild Life for landing her the role of Lorraine, Marty's mother, because "they were looking at Eric Stoltz for Marty McFly, and they were, like, 'Who's that girl?'" she told The A.V. Club. "So that's how I got the first audition for that."

25. In the original script, Lorraine's name was Meg.

26. To achieve Lorraine's 1985 look, Thompson's prosthetic makeup took three and a half hours to apply.

27. In 2015, footage of Stoltz as Marty was released for the first time in a documentary included on the 30th anniversary Blu-ray set. "We wanted to soft pedal that," Gale said of the decision to release a small look at his performance. "We didn't want to make Eric feel bad."

28. Back to the Future: The Animated series ran for two seasons, airing on CBS from 1991 until 1992.

29. In March 2020, the musical adaptation of Back to the Future made its debut in England, with Olly Dobson as Marty McFly and Tony winner Roger Bart as Dr. Emmett Brown. It eventually made its way to Broadway, ending an 18-month run in January 2025.

30. Zemeckis and Gale are firmly against the idea of a fourth film, with the director saying on a Zoom cast reunion that, "If I had an idea which I could have pitched to Bob [Gale] with a straight face, we would have made it."

#636. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#637. Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend

Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends

After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. Niall McVeigh

Ipswich v Nottingham Forest, Friday 8pm BST

It was five months ago but it feels a lot longer. When these two sides met in May to finish the season, the contest doubled as Pep Guardiola’s leaving party after 10 years in the job and twice as many trophies, an era now laden with asterisks. It must be surreal for Aston Villa supporters, too. Their 2-1 victory at the Etihad Stadium, inspired by two goals from Ollie Watkins to complete a league double over City, came only four days after their Europa League triumph in Istanbul, where Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Emi Buendía were the scorers. Buendía is the only one left in claret and blue as Unai Emery builds a new side, one that has picked up in form after a single point from their first four league games. City, meanwhile, are thriving on the pitch: victory would make them just the third side to win their first eight games of a Premier League season. Taha Hashim

Aston Villa v Manchester City, Saturday 12.30pm BST

Max Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history with his dazzling solo strike against Everton at the Emirates in March. But the supremely talented 16-year-old has found opportunities limited this season. Dowman has played only nine minutes in the Premier League despite scoring twice against Ipswich in the Carabao Cup last month as Arsenal have tried to protect their rising star. Yet the suspected quad muscle injury suffered by Bukayo Saka in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich means Mikel Arteta is short of attacking options. With David Moyes’s side back in north London, it could be the perfect chance for Dowman to step up in his favoured position on the right flank. Ed Aarons

Coventry and Fulham have only met twice in the English top flight – back in 1967-68, when the promoted Sky Blues took a single point from two meetings, but stayed up by a point while Fulham went down. It is too early to call Saturday’s game a six-pointer in the relegation battle, but the two teams sit either side of the dreaded dotted line after shaky starts. Coventry have shown glimpses of their Championship swagger, particularly in the 4-1 rout of Newcastle, but Frank Lampard wants his players to start thinking like a Premier League team. “I can’t keep applauding the players, believing they deserve to be here,” the Coventry manager said. “Now we have to get over that. We can’t be too soft.” Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich all visit the CBS Arena in the coming weeks, so there is an opportunity to consolidate. Fulham were linked with Lampard in the summer, and questions remain over whether Álvaro Arbeloa is pragmatic or flexible enough to succeed. Will these sides meet in the Premier League again next season? The jury is out. NM

Tottenham’s recent record against Chelsea is miserable. They are on a six-match losing streak against their London rivals and have collected a paltry two points at Stamford Bridge since last winning there in April 2018. Tottenham finally have a league win – they beat Coventry 3-1 on Monday – but remain unconvincing. Roberto De Zerbi used a 3-4-2-1 system against Coventry. He had problems in midfield but now has to work out whether to change a winning team. Does he stick with James Maddison after the No 10’s excellent goal against his boyhood club? Spurs still looked short of energy at times. There is an argument to bring back Conor Gallagher’s dynamism, but would that hurt the side’s quality on the ball? Mateus Fernandes is another option but is yet to establish himself since joining from West Ham. Spurs’ approach remains hard to decipher. De Zerbi likes possession, but Chelsea want teams to open up as the Blues have searing pace on the break. Given their history in this fixture it seems Spurs should focus on tightening up. Equally they can’t be passive and need a threat on the break. De Zerbi will be searching for the right balance. Jacob Steinberg

Talk of Brighton achieving Champions League qualification for the first time will gain more credence, even at this early stage, should Fabian Hürzeler’s confident side extend their unbeaten run to nine matches in all competitions. There have been six clean sheets and 23 goals scored in sequence that featured six wins in a row and the Premier League’s highest scorers will take encouragement from Liverpool’s defensive problems in the comeback against Villarreal, which were not limited to Virgil van Dijk’s early lapses. Andoni Iraola is yet to savour a first home league win as Liverpool head coach – Anfield has seen only four home wins in 13 league games this year – and he will be wary of Brighton’s various threats. But with Rio Ngumoha electric in the Champions League win, Florian Wirtz improving and Alexander Isak increasingly decisive, the ingredients are in place for another enthralling spectacle. Andy Hunter

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Who can or will lift Manchester United after the latest dismal/embarrassing week? Bruno Fernandes’s abdication of captaincy duties – accusing his manager of being tactically inept – showed what a rabble the team has become under Michael Carrick; and beyond the double footballer of the year, is there another star act who can win a game? Bournemouth will hope to take advantage, register only a second league win of the season, and deepen the misery for their hosts and fans. If his side goes down to the Cherries, Carrick will surely follow: the latest victim of the United circus. Jamie Jackson

Manchester United v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm GMT

It’s been six months since Crystal Palace recorded a clean sheet in the Premier League at Selhurst Park and the pressure will be on Pierre Sage against Newcastle on Sunday. Palace have conceded eight goals in four home league games this season, although they welcome back Axel Disasi from suspension after his reckless red card against Ipswich. The French defender was brought in on loan from Chelsea to add experience but cost Palace in the defeat by the newly-promoted side and had to watch from the sidelines as the Eagles were humiliated against Brighton last weekend. Disasi owes Sage a favour and he will be desperate to make up for his poor start to life in south London. EA

Crystal Palace v Newcastle, Sunday 2pm GMT

Something unusual will happen at the MKM Stadium on Sunday; either Hull City or Brentford will register more than 50% possession. In seven league games, Brentford only had more of the ball in their 1-1 draw at Leeds. The hosts, meanwhile, are comfortably the most possession-averse team in the top flight so far this season, at an average of just over 30%. Both teams have been effective on the break and successful at set-pieces, with three goals apiece from dead balls. This may prove to be a match for the purists, where one clinical moment makes the difference. The Bees head coach, Keith Andrews, will hope it comes from Igor Thiago, yet to recapture the prolific form of last season. “Thiago at the moment is a very marked man, but we’ve got goalscorers throughout the team,” Andrews said of the Brazilian forward, who has scored one goal in seven this season. “Thiago being Thiago wants to score more goals, and he’s certainly not far away.” NM

Nordi Mukiele ranks among Sunderland’s best players and most influential dressing-room figures. Tellingly the former Paris Saint-Germain defender has been scathing about his team’s dismal start to the Premier League campaign and expects a reaction when Leeds visit Wearside on Sunday. “Leeds will be the right moment to show everyone we are not dead,” says Mukiele, well aware that Régis Le Bris’s side start this weekend on the bottom of the table. “We have not been good enough. Right now it’s not us; we are not Sunderland. I believe we can go back to the top. I believe in this team and this staff. We have quality.” Sunderland must use their three league fixtures before the international break – Leeds, Coventry away and Chelsea at home – to remind everyone why they finished seventh last season. Louise Taylor

#638. President Trump says he called Googles CEO to rename the Atlantic Ocean

Rising gas prices. The Iran War. AI's effects on the economy.

Across the United States, Americans are worried about a multitude of major challenges.

On Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he called Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google, one of the biggest tech companies on the planet, to discuss a pressing issue that's been on his mind: Changing the name of the Atlantic Ocean.

At a rally in South Carolina, Trump shared that after successfully getting Google Maps to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America, he tried to pressure the tech giant to do the same for the Atlantic Ocean.

“We have a lake and we have a gulf, now we need a river and we need an ocean," Trump said at the rally, as reported by the Washington Post.

Trump said that he “called Google Maps," which he described as "really great with the lake" regarding his prior requests.

"They're still rattled from the Gulf," Trump said, adding that he called Pichai because he wanted to see if Google would be up to changing the name of the Atlantic Ocean too.

"Sundar, I'm thinking of the Atlantic Ocean," Trump claimed he said in the call.

However, it seems that renaming the Atlantic Ocean as the American Ocean was one step too far for Google, which has previously kowtowed to Trump's geographical demands. (Google's previous Google Maps changes only appear for U.S. visitors to the platform)

"No, no, no. This time, I’m not doing it," Pichai said, according to Trump's version of events. "Please don’t ask us to do that."

According to Trump, Pichai's reasoning was that "oceans are different" because they "cover a lot of countries."

After the call, Trump said he'd "probably pass" on renaming the Atlantic Ocean after his call with Google. The tech giant has yet to confirm the call with the president occurred.

"I think let's keep it the Atlantic Ocean, right?" Trump told rallygoers, before turning his attention to the West Coast.

"Pacific Ocean," Trump added. "We're going to call it the American Ocean."
